text: Desktop Control Enablement conditions for Desktop Control, coordinates and the 17 actions (including the wait observation), typetext focus/newline semantics, how screenshots are appended to the model, failure diagnosis, and rollback boundaries. 桌面控制 exists for targets whose only entry point is a graphical interface: if commands, files, or browser tools can solve it, do not go through desktop control, because it is slower, more error-prone, and it directly drives the user's real screen. It both drives and observes: it injects mouse/keyboard actions and then screenshots; to just see the desktop's current state, or to confirm whether the previous action took effect, use the wait action — it waits and then screenshots without injecting any input. | Canonical name | Aliases | | --- | --- | | 桌面控制 | desktopcontrol, desktop | Prerequisites All three must hold: 1. The installed build was compiled with desktop control enabled (it is off by default). 2. You are in desktop mode and have explicitly turned the desktop control switch on (it is off by default). 3. The current model supports vision; otherwise desktop control and the image-reading tool are both filtered out. Across the forms: the Desktop (desktop mode) lists this tool in its extra-enabled set by default; under the Server, Cloud, and CLI forms desktop control is unavailable. Arguments One call needs an action; pointer actions also need a position: Position uses normalized coordinates: either an [x1,y1,x2,y2] tuple or a two-value center point. Coordinates are based on a default 1000×1000 normalized grid; at run time the center is taken and mapped linearly onto real screen pixels. There are 17 actions: leftclick, leftdoubleclick, rightclick, middleclick; lefthold / righthold / middlehold and their matching leftrelease / rightrelease / middlerelease; scrolldown / scrollup; presskey, typetext, wait, movemouse, dragdrop. Related arguments: a key uses key, typed text uses text, a wait uses delayms, drag duration uses durationms (about 400 ms when omitted), scroll steps use scrollsteps, and a drag destination uses tobbox. typetext may omit bbox: it then types into the control that already has focus and does not click again, which fits the usual "click the field, then type" flow. With bbox, the pointer is placed there first. Newlines become Enter and tabs become Tab; CRLF counts as one Enter. Every action accepts only its own fields; extra or cross-action fields are rejected. Coordinates are bounded to 0..10000, and text and key lengths are bounded too. Waiting and observing The wait action reads desktop windows and screen state. Give a wait duration (delayms, 0–30000 ms; anything larger is clamped to 30000); a screenshot follows when the wait completes. This wait is the observation semantics, not a UI animation. Automatic behavior It takes a screenshot after every action. A non-wait action first gets at least 240 ms to settle, then frames are compared every 80 ms and capture stops as soon as the screen is stable, after at most three probes. This lets window changes, menus, and input echoes appear without blocking indefinitely. wait uses only its explicit delayms. After a successful return, the orchestrator assembles the screenshots into a user-role multimodal message appended to the model: a text hint plus the screenshot from before the action (if any) and the current screenshot, so the tool result the model sees contains no image itself and the picture arrives through that appended message. Budget a task as "one action = one call + one look". A single screenshot entering context is capped at 8 MiB, and exceeding that fails. No action hint animation is shown. A screenshot is captured with the bounded stabilization policy above and returned as the observation receipt. The result fields actionapplied, screenshotafteraction, and observationready indicate that the action was issued and the current screenshot is ready for verification. Check the screenshot first and retry the same action only when the state is confirmed unchanged. Errors Desktop control not compiled in: the call fails outright and says the capability is not enabled. Not in desktop mode, or the switch is off: it returns "desktop control is disabled". Missing arguments: action is required; pointer actions must include a position, while typetext may omit it. A malformed position reports an illegal coordinate. Screenshot failure: capture times out after 5000 ms by default (100 ms minimum), and failure reports an error upward. Boundaries Actions are real input injection with no rollback. lefthold and leftrelease must be used in pairs, or the mouse state may be left dangling; dragdrop is press, smooth move, release. Coordinates change with resolution; normalized coordinates only guarantee consistency between one observation and the action that follows it, so observe again after switching screens or changing resolution. A screenshot is also saved to the user's container directory; a persistence failure only logs a warning and does not affect the result. The screenshot directory keeps frames by count, holding only the most recent few (3 by default), so temporary files do not pile up without bound. Authorization follows least privilege: it needs an explicit user switch, it does not silently capture the screen in the background, and it does not expose system capabilities to a remote party. Prerequisites Arguments Waiting and observing Automatic behavior Errors Boundaries

title: Subagent Control
summary: The 11 actions and dispatch parameters of `subagent_control`, context inheritance rules, single versus batch dispatch, wait and report semantics, and target resolution with its per-call caps.
text: Subagent Control The 11 actions and dispatch parameters of subagentcontrol, context inheritance rules, single versus batch dispatch, wait and report semantics, and target resolution with its per-call caps. The tool is subagentcontrol. A subagent is a unit of work the main agent creates temporarily: it dispatches one task thread and reclaims it once the task ends. This is currently the only form of collaboration. All of these actions hang off the current thread; creating, switching, and archiving threads themselves is a separate matter, handled by Thread Control. Actions Each call specifies one action. Actions use closed, action-specific field branches; cross-action fields are rejected (for example, list cannot receive message, and spawn cannot receive waitseconds). list: list the child threads under a parent thread. history: read the message history of a child thread. send: append a round of instructions to a child thread. report: a child thread reports back to its parent (only a subagent can do this). spawn: dispatch one subagent. batchspawn: dispatch a batch at once, with a strategy and handling for the remaining branches. status: read a target's current snapshot without waiting. wait: wait until the completion condition is met or a timeout occurs. interrupt: cancel a run. close: close a session, optionally cascading. resume: restore it to active; with a message it is the same as one append instruction. When no target is given, the current session is treated as the parent thread by default; you can also point at a target using a dispatched run id, session id, or batch id. When dispatching, you can also specify: label: a recognizable name for the child thread. agentid, model: override the subagent or the model it uses; both are checked against the current user's agent ownership. runtimeoutseconds: the timeout of a single run; in a synchronous dispatch it is also the wait duration. forkturns: copy the most recent rounds of user context, 0–16, 0 by default. contextsummary: attach a background summary. cleanup: how to wrap up, keep (the default) or delete (runtime state is cleaned up and the child is closed; its history remains inspectable). Context inheritance The copied context and background summary are reference data and never change the subagent's system prompt: the parent thread's most recent rounds are prepended to the task text as quoted background, copying at most 256 history entries and 64 KiB in total, with anything beyond marked as truncated. A forkturns above 16, or a summary above 16384 bytes, fails immediately; when forkturns is 0 and no summary is written, no history is read. A subagent inherits its parent session's tool set by default, and its tool system prompt stays frozen once it is first determined; long-term memory and background injection happen only once, at initialization. Single and batch dispatch One: when the timeout is 0 or negative it returns at once and runs in the background; when it is positive it waits synchronously for a result, sending progress every 5 seconds and returning a timeout if the wait expires. A batch: context is prepared for every task first, and if any single preparation fails the whole batch is not dispatched (no half batch is left behind). It then dispatches one by one, reclaiming any that fails to start and marking it failed. The completion condition follows the strategy: run all in parallel / review then merge → wait for all; first success → finished at the first success. Once it finishes early, the remaining branches are kept by default, or interrupted by default under the first-success strategy. Waiting, reporting, and interrupting A wait subscribes to the completion signal first, and when there is no signal it polls at a fixed interval that settles around one second (between 0.2 and 5 seconds). A wait can end for three reasons: the completion condition is met, it times out, or the parent thread receives a message. When a child thread is running its current turn and its mailbox is open, a message sent to it goes straight into that turn; otherwise it starts a new one, and sending a message to itself raises an error. When a child reports back, an idle parent thread is woken automatically to receive it, and submitting the same message again does not enqueue it a second time. An interrupt only requests cancellation of the run and does not change session state; a close sets the session state to closed and cancels the run along with it, and can also cascade to its descendants; a resume sets the state back to active. Target resolution and caps A single call can select at most 200 targets; beyond that it reports that there are too many targets. Single-target actions such as reading history or sending a message require exactly one child thread: it first looks up by exact id, then looks for a unique close name under the same parent thread, then falls back to picking the only child thread when there is just one; if it is still not unique it errors and asks you to use the exact id returned by a dispatch or a list. A target must share the same root as the caller, and the root thread cannot be a dispatch target; nesting depth is capped at 32 levels. A batch holds at most 64 tasks; beyond that the whole batch is rejected rather than truncated. Each child thread's outbound messages and receipt cache are bounded, and a full one is treated as a rejection; a list holds at most 200 entries, 50 by default. Model-facing result previews and status messages in an entry are truncated to 4000 characters; the full content is available from the history or that child thread's trail. In Desktop this tool is on by default as an extra; the other forms require an administrator to select it. Actions Context inheritance Single and batch dispatch Waiting, reporting, and interrupting Target resolution and caps

title: Thread Control
summary: The eight actions and available fields of `thread_control`, the four listing scopes, persistence behavior of writes and switches, ownership checks and list caps, and how it is exposed per form.
text: Thread Control The eight actions and available fields of threadcontrol, the four listing scopes, persistence behavior of writes and switches, ownership checks and list caps, and how it is exposed per form. The tool is threadcontrol, also known as sessionthread. A single agent can hold several independent task threads at once, and scheduling, locking, and live status are all isolated per thread. This tool manages the task threads themselves; the temporary units of work that a subagent dispatches and reclaims once done are a different matter, covered in Subagent Control. The thread and round model is described in Sessions and Rounds. Actions When the user raises a separate, independent matter, carry it with a new thread rather than continuing in the current one. Switching between threads, going back to a parent thread, renaming, archiving, and restoring all go through this tool too. Each call specifies one action. Model calls use closed, action-specific field branches; each action accepts only relevant fields, runtime validation rejects unknown fields again, and list/lifecycle actions return only the necessary thread summary: list: list threads by scope. info: view a single thread's details, together with its parent thread and direct child threads. create: create a thread, inheriting the parent thread's agent and tool overrides by default. switch: switch to a given thread. back: switch back to the current thread's parent thread. updatetitle: change the title. archive / restore: archive / restore. The available fields are sessionid (the target thread, the current thread by default), parentsessionid (used only when creating, the current thread by default), title (for creating or renaming; when omitted on creation the thread is called "New session" by default), scope, status, and limit. Listing scopes scope decides which threads are listed: branch (the default): the ancestor chain from the root to the current thread, plus the current thread and its direct child threads; each one is marked as an ancestor, the current thread, or a child. children: the direct child threads of the target thread. roots: the root threads that have no parent thread. all: all threads by status and agent scope. Each thread in the list shows which one it is, its status, and when its latest message arrived. The "runtime status" there comes from live in-memory monitoring and is not the same measure as the persisted "active / archived". Automatic behavior A newly created thread inherits the parent thread's agent and tool overrides. Archiving, restoring, and switching write the change to storage and refresh the session's modification time. When archiving is combined with switching away, it picks another active thread under the same agent to switch to. Errors A missing user identity, a target thread that does not exist, a rename with no title, or a "back to parent" when the current thread has no parent all raise clear errors. Viewing details, switching, archiving, and restoring all check agent ownership; an explicitly given agent that does not match the target thread is rejected as a permission error. A list holds at most 200 entries, and expanding child threads is bound by the same limit. The "switch away while archiving" only happens when switching is enabled and another active thread really exists under the same agent, and it picks the first other thread in the list, which may not be the intended one. A rename forces the status of a non-archived thread back to active. Switching threads is not the same as switching work: scheduling and locks are isolated per thread, and a thread you switch to that is running shows its status in live monitoring. It never deletes a thread; archiving is reversible and a restore brings it back. Form differences Desktop lists this tool as a system-level hidden tool, in neither the default set nor the desktop selectable set; Cloud, CLI, and Server expose it according to the administrator's selection. Actions Listing scopes Automatic behavior Errors Form differences

title: Memory Manager
summary: The seven actions of `memory_manager`, the short-index-injection plus fetch-on-demand usage pattern, a write example, and field constraints.
text: Memory Manager The seven actions of memorymanager, the short-index-injection plus fetch-on-demand usage pattern, a write example, and field constraints. memorymanager manages the current agent's long-term memory within the current user scope, with seven supported actions: list, search, get, add, update, remove, clear. Each action has a closed field branch: list/search reject write fields, get is the only full-content read, and writes/deletes return only an id and status. Injection and retrieval By default the system prompt receives only a short index (memory id plus title); the full content is not injected along with it. When detail is needed, first use list / search to find the memory id, then use get to fetch the full text. Keep memory ids within 8 characters when possible, so they are easy to search and locate. add / update use only the current core fields: title, content, tag, related memory id, and memory time. Actions list: returns recent memory indexes, 30 by default. Each entry contains id, title, tag, and update time. search: matches on title or content, 10 by default. A match includes a snippet and whether it matched in the title or the content. get: reads the full content by id, and also returns the related memory id and memory time. add: adds one entry, given title, content, tag, and memory time together. update: updates by id. remove: removes by id. clear: clears everything. Write example: Boundaries The old summary, tags, entities, and category are no longer recommended inputs. list / search are the main retrieval actions, and get is the only action that reads full detail. Writes only affect later new threads; they do not write back into the system prompt of a thread that is already frozen. Injection and retrieval Actions Boundaries

title: Schedule Task
summary: The eight actions and common fields of `schedule_task`, its two execution threads, concurrency and missed-run policy for recurring jobs, and failure diagnosis around queries and the scheduler switch.
text: Schedule Task The eight actions and common fields of scheduletask, its two execution threads, concurrency and missed-run policy for recurring jobs, and failure diagnosis around queries and the scheduler switch. Use it when something should not be done only once but repeated on a fixed cadence, or when it should run automatically once at a designated moment: it creates, changes, inspects, runs right away, and enables or disables jobs. Actions and fields A call specifies the action and the job's content. The model schema is action-specific: add/update expose job fields, get/remove/enable/disable/run require only jobid, and list/status reject job fields. The flat form uses top-level fields: For precise control over timing, use a nested time rule, which takes a cron expression and a time zone. Use schedule or scheduletext only for actions that accept scheduling fields; query and control actions reject them: Supported actions: add (create), update (change), remove (delete), enable / disable (enable or disable), get (view one), list (list), run (run once right away), and status (scheduler status). Common fields: action: the action to perform. jobid: the job's identifier, used for changing, deleting, enabling or disabling, running right away, and querying. name: the job's display name. scheduletext: the time rule, written in natural language or cron text. schedule: used only when you need to express precisely "at a moment / every so often / cron". message: the message sent to the agent when the job fires. session: which thread the job runs in, main or isolated only. enabled: whether the job is enabled right after creation. Execution threads session decides where this happens: main: runs in the thread the job is bound to. By default it is bound to the thread you created the job in; switching pages later, opening a new thread, or another thread becoming active does not change the binding. When busy it queues into the shared task queue, and you can also stop it from the bound thread. isolated: runs in a fresh child thread under the bound thread. The result is delivered back to the bound thread as a standalone "completed turn" rather than being fed to the model again as a new user instruction; the child thread and the result turn each have their own identity, and an error does not get written into the previous turn's assistant bubble. If the bound thread is archived or deleted, or its owning agent does not match, the job fails explicitly rather than quietly picking another thread to stand in. Concurrency of recurring jobs A single recurring job has at most one run active at any moment. Even if it is written as once per second while a single run takes far longer than a second, it will not fan out into a pile of identical concurrent jobs. Missed intervals are skipped or coalesced, and the next run time is pushed forward again from the current time: the behavior keeps the latest cadence rather than catching up on every missed run. Errors run returning queued: true only means the asynchronous run has been accepted, not that it has finished. Do not repeatedly poll for it within the turn that created the job; finish the current reply first. Querying a job shows the thread it is bound to, whether it is running, and its last result and last error; it displays local-time-zone time, the run rule, and the bound thread, while the raw result stays in the thread log. When a time rule provides both scheduletext and schedule, schedule wins; the smallest interval is 1 second. Arguments must be complete JSON; if it is not closed, the arguments are reported invalid directly. The server must have scheduling enabled first. When it is off, create, update, enable, and manual run return explicit errors, but the job list can still be read and the scheduler status still shown; a service already running needs a config reload or restart to pick up the change. Scheduled runs inherit the approval mode, model, tool capabilities, and workspace configuration of the owning user and agent. An isolated thread keeps the bound thread's explicit tool restrictions and freezes its own starting tool baseline, and still obeys the user's tool permissions: an agent that requires approval does not become fully automatic just because a schedule triggered it. Actions and fields Execution threads Concurrency of recurring jobs Errors

title: Goal State
summary: The six `goal` actions and their required fields, revision-based concurrency, authority by turn origin, the user-only creation boundary, and how the common failures read.
text: Goal State The six goal actions and their required fields, revision-based concurrency, authority by turn origin, the user-only creation boundary, and how the common failures read. # Goal State A goal pins one objective to a session so the agent keeps pushing it forward whenever the session goes idle. Users start goals; on the model side there is only the goal tool, used to read and advance a goal that already exists. Actions | Action | What it does | Required fields | | --- | --- | --- | | get | Read the current goal, its phase, and its revision | action | | edit | Change the objective or the continuation-round cap | action, goalid, revision, objective | | pause | Pause and stop auto-continuation | action, goalid, revision | | resume | Resume and re-arm | same as above | | complete | Mark it complete | same as above | | blocked | Report a blocker | same as above plus blockedreason | There is no create action. Only the user starts or replaces a goal — via /goal, the goal bar, or the goal API. If an older client sends a create request, the runtime rejects it and tells the model to hand that decision back to the user. Revision concurrency Every change bumps the revision. All mutating actions must send the goalid and the exact revision that get returned; a mismatch is rejected, so auto-continuation rounds and human interventions never overwrite each other. Call get right before writing instead of reusing a revision remembered from an earlier round. An edit objective is capped at 4000 characters. maxgoalrounds accepts 1 to 10000 and cannot drop below the rounds already started. Authority What a turn may do depends on where it came from: | Turn origin | Allowed actions | | --- | --- | | Direct human request | get, edit, pause, resume, complete, blocked | | This goal's own auto-continuation round | get, complete, blocked | So changing the objective, pausing, and resuming — decisions that belong to the human — only work in a human turn. An auto-continuation round can only wrap up or report a blocker. Failure reads Stale revision: call get for the current value and retry with it, not with the old arguments. edit / pause / resume inside an auto-continuation round: authority is insufficient; wait for the user. blocked rejected for too few rounds: the same blocking condition has to persist for at least 3 consecutive continuation rounds. Difficulty, uncertainty, or useful remaining work is not a blocker. A goal that stopped moving: check the phase and the armed state. Armed is in-process only, so after a restart or a session resume an active goal still needs one resume before it continues. Where this page stops Phase, round budget, and the continuation gate are designed on Goal State System; the goal banner, the goal bar, and the /goal command are covered on each form's usage page. This page only covers how to call the tool. Goal State Actions Revision concurrency Authority Failure reads Where this page stops

title: MCP
summary: The two MCP directions — `server@tool` registration and routing for external servers, packing mode and the streamable-http limit, plus the outgoing `/wunder/mcp` endpoint and common failures.
text: MCP The two MCP directions — server@tool registration and routing for external servers, packing mode and the streamable-http limit, plus the outgoing /wunder/mcp endpoint and common failures. # MCP MCP is the common protocol between wunder and external tool services. It runs in two directions with separate entry points and configuration: pulling an external service in for the model, and exposing wunder to an outside system. Pulling in an external service Declare a name, an address, and a transport in configuration, switch it on, and its tools appear in the tool catalog. One transport only: streamable-http. stdio is not supported on the wunder side, and older transport values are rejected when listing or calling tools. Registered as server@tool: every allowed tool appears under that name, and any name containing @ is treated as MCP. Packing mode: mark a server as packed and it folds into one tool with three actions — list available tools, read one tool's description, call one tool. Dozens of details stay out of the context until asked for. List cache: valid for 30 seconds, at most 128 entries. Object arguments only: a non-object argument is treated as no arguments. Result shape: a direct call returns the MCP service's own result; a call routed through a user-tool alias gets the shared shell wrapped around it. The allow list is checked on every call, packed or not: a tool that is not allowed never appears and cannot be called. Exposing wunder wunder is also an MCP server: the Server and Desktop mount an endpoint at /wunder/mcp over Streamable HTTP, and wunder negotiates the protocol version itself. | Tool | What it does | | --- | --- | | excute | Runs one agent task and returns the final reply (the name really is spelled this way) | | doc2md | Parses a document and returns Markdown | When the endpoint runs a task it computes the tool set for that agent and removes itself from it, so an endpoint-driven agent cannot call the endpoint back. Address and verification details are on MCP Endpoint. Common failures | Symptom | Check first | | --- | --- | | Server configured, no tools | Whether it is enabled, whether the allow list blocks it, whether the transport value is stale | | "Old transport type no longer supported" | Switch to streamable-http | | "Unknown built-in tool" | The name is not a canonical name or alias, has no @, is not a skill, and is not a knowledge base | | A user tool "took over" a built-in name | Alias routing wins over built-in dispatch; this is expected | Boundaries MCP tools get no bypass: they join built-in tools, skills, and knowledge bases in one tool view, and pass the ability selection set and model availability filters like everything else. Dynamically registered names share one table with built-ins — avoid built-in canonical names and aliases when naming servers and tools. Knowledge bases register by name too; see Tools Overview. Skills live on Skills. MCP Pulling in an external service Exposing wunder Common failures Boundaries

title: Skills
summary: What a skill is (a directory, `SKILL.md`, an entry script), its two uses, skill names and the `owner@skill` form, mounting and ability selection, and the 60-second subprocess boundary.
text: Skills What a skill is (a directory, SKILL.md, an entry script), its two uses, skill names and the owner@skill form, mounting and ability selection, and the 60-second subprocess boundary. # Skills A skill packages knowledge and scripts: one directory, a SKILL.md with frontmatter (name, description), and an entry script looked up in a fixed order. It works both as a callable tool and as reference material you only read. Two uses | Use | Path | Good for | | --- | --- | --- | | Call it as a tool | The skill name is itself a callable tool name | You already know which skill to use | | Read its body | 技能调用 (alias skillcall) returns name, description, path, root, and body | You want the workflow or only its knowledge before deciding | 技能调用 replaces skill-root placeholders in the body with real paths, so the model can read files and run scripts with what it gets back. It does not run the entry script — execution is a separate call. Names and ownership A bare name (文稿校对) is a skill you have. A skill shared by someone else is written owner@skill. On a name collision wunder does not guess: it reports the ambiguity and lists the candidates. Entry script Looked up in order run.py → skill.py → main.py, first hit wins. Importing a skill package (archives and collisions included) is the platform's job, so a script never has to unpack itself. The global skill directory comes from configuration, and the script executor path can be overridden. Mounting and selection Built-in skills ship with the package and are marked apart from your own; user skills route by name like MCP servers and knowledge bases. "Selecting an ability" only puts a tool or skill name into that agent's selection set; the skill layer still does the executing. Model availability filters apply before anything reaches the context, and thresholds differ per capability. Execution boundary A skill runs as a subprocess executing a script, with a 60-second timeout, inheriting the platform's path and permission boundary. Do not put privileged operations in a skill script. If it will not run, first check that the entry script exists, then whether 技能调用 can read the body at all — if it cannot, the directory or the frontmatter is usually the problem. For MCP see MCP; the overall name-routing rules are on Tools Overview. Skills Two uses Names and ownership Entry script Mounting and selection Execution boundary

title: Architecture
summary: One core and engine shared by the forms, the fixed path a message takes inside a session, storage choices, bounded views, external interfaces, and runtime defaults.
text: Architecture One core and engine shared by the forms, the fixed path a message takes inside a session, storage choices, bounded views, external interfaces, and runtime defaults. All forms — Desktop, Android, Cloud, CLI, and Server — share the same core and engine, differing only at the access layer. Real execution happens inside sessions, and the interface reads a bounded display view that is paginated and carries a byte budget. Layers : the three local forms call the shared engine in-process; Cloud and Admin reuse the same engine through the server. The engine depends on the core, while storage and runtime ship with each form. Forms and Delivery | Form | How it is delivered | Interface | | --- | --- | --- | | Desktop | A desktop app; the engine ships inside the local process and calls in-process by default without local HTTP | Native UI, compiled into the app | | Android | An APK; the engine ships inside the local process and calls the shared engine in-process | Native UI (Slint), reusing the Desktop components | | Cloud | A web app; its build artifacts are served read-only by a separate web service, not hosted by the Server itself | Single-page app | | CLI | A command-line program; when terminal conditions are not met it degrades to one-shot execution instead of the full-screen interactive interface | Terminal UI | | Server | A server process, mounting Admin and a few static directories | Admin (no build step) | Message Path From the moment you send a message to the moment the final reply is stored, the order is fixed: | Step | What it does | | --- | --- | | Access | The main chat channel takes the request and can submit, resume, observe, cancel, and approve it | | Admission | The session runtime decides whether to run it immediately or queue it — the single decision point for "dispatch or queue" | | Record the user round | A user round is allocated idempotently; this is the only write entry for the session record | | Prepare the request | Context, visible tools, and the system prompt are assembled, and a decision is made on whether to freeze | | Main loop | Every model call increments the model round by one | | Run tools | Policy and approval, hooks, timeouts, and budget come first, then the call is dispatched to the actual tool | | Final reply | Multiple refreshes within the same model round update the same visible output item and never append duplicate bubbles | | Real-time push | Emitting an event writes to the persistence layer synchronously, and subscribers are notified only after the write completes | Three places that are easy to mislocate: The status registry the interface queries for a session's current state is a different thing from the session runtime that actually runs execution. In-process wake signals only exist to accelerate; across multiple instances, correctness comes from polling convergence, not from them. The four phases of a tool — pre, execute, post, result — are only a descriptive model; hooks are off by default and are not part of the execution main chain. Data and Storage Storage is split by purpose: thread logs, sessions, workspaces, memory fragments, and so on each form their own group, and the engine depends only on this set of interfaces without caring which database sits underneath. For the choice of database: with no configuration it is SQLite, and configured as PostgreSQL it runs on PostgreSQL. There is no version table and no migration-script directory. Tables are created idempotently on startup and new columns are detected at startup, so there is no such thing as migrating by version number. Every kind of record — sessions, round tails, workspaces, media attachments, memory fragments, knowledge vectors, users and quotas, channel bindings, interop shadows — is defined together. Bounded Views What you see is a bounded display view, not a full history you can page through to the end, and not a complete snapshot of execution. | View | Per page | Cap | Response budget | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Chat page (one row per user round) | 12 | 20 | 128 KB | | Thread trace page (per entry) | 80 | 100 | 192 KB | | Body chunks | 8 KB per chunk | — | fetched on demand | The mechanisms that go with it: a write also produces a projection table and a truncated preview; when a projection is not ready it falls back to a bounded window over the source table; background rebuilds stay at no more than 1% duty cycle; and each change push fetches 200 items. The machinery that measures historical usage and budgets for context compression does not handle pagination. External Interfaces | Surface | Fact | | --- | --- | | HTTP | Routes share the /wunder/ prefix, and error responses have exactly one source format | | WebSocket | Six channels: chat, the core request surface, gateway, interop tunnel, interop remote observer, and world / LAN | | Gateway | Not an HTTP gateway, but an access registry plus targeted RPC plus online-presence broadcast; its only transport is /wunder/gateway/ws | | Channels | Adapter registration; a bounded inbound queue, and a persistent outbound outbox with backoff retry | | Interop | Local nodes are outbound-only; one tunnel carries three planes; capabilities are tiered L0–L3, and the default device capability set excludes L3 | | MCP | The Server has a built-in service endpoint at /wunder/mcp (streamable-http), and external MCP clients are registered in configuration | Runtime Defaults | Item | Default | | --- | --- | | Server listen | 0.0.0.0:8000, overridable by environment variable or configuration | | Active session cap | 300 (unlimited for administrators) | | Session lock | 120 s timeout, 5 s heartbeat | | Model / tool timeout | 120 s each | | Model round cap | 1000 for non-administrators | Limits "The Cloud page is hosted by the Server." No. The Server mounts only Admin and a few static directories; Cloud's build artifacts are served by a separate web service. "The front end needs several fetches to get the full history." The front end was never meant to get the full history; it consumes a paginated view and fetches body chunks on demand. "Desktop calls its own backend over local HTTP." By default it is a native in-process call; the standalone compatibility bridge is kept only for existing clients. "Swarm orchestration is still part of the architecture." The engine and scheduling surface no longer have this module, and the empty directories have been deleted; session write permission is always writable. title: Goal
summary: The driver tools of goal mode, its four phases, the default 256-round cap, and CAS-on-revision updates.
text: Goal The driver tools of goal mode, its four phases, the default 256-round cap, and CAS-on-revision updates. # Goal A goal is attached to a session; the agent keeps working on it until the goal completes, becomes blocked, or exhausts the round budget. Driver tools | Tool | Role | | --- | --- | | goal | Uses action=get|edit|pause|resume|complete|blocked to read, edit, pause, resume, complete, or report blocked; only the user can create a goal | Phases Four values: active, paused, blocked, complete. Updates use CAS-on-revision: an update must carry the goal's current revision, and a mismatch is rejected. Started rounds only ever increase. Defaults | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Goal round cap | 256 | | Automatic blocking after no progress | 3 rounds | Entry points | Entry | Location | | --- | --- | | Interface | /wunder/chat/sessions/{id}/goal | | Slash command | /goal | Limits There is no token budget and no cooldown between rounds. Whether a goal stops depends on three things only: the round budget, the phase, and whether it is armed. The armed state is not persisted: after a process restart or a session resume, even if the phase is still active, an explicit goal action=resume is needed to arm it again. When a goal stops moving, check armed first. The desktop form does not expose goal selection; the runtime injects it per session. The Admin has no goal UI; goal operations happen in the Cloud, the Desktop, and the CLI. Goal Driver tools Phases Defaults Entry points Limits

title: Context Compression
summary: The four graded compression levels triggered when the context window is exceeded, what compression protects and leaves alone, compression records, and the local-reduction path that comes first.
text: Context Compression The four graded compression levels triggered when the context window is exceeded, what compression protects and leaves alone, compression records, and the local-reduction path that comes first. How much history a single conversation can carry is set by the model's context window. As a conversation grows, the total of history plus tool results can exceed the ceiling, and compression trims the history without interrupting the conversation so it keeps running. Compression is not deletion. Deletion cuts content outright, regardless of importance; compression reorganizes content, keeping the key facts and trimming the redundant parts. Triggers These situations tend to trigger compression: a very long conversation (dozens of rounds or more), a tool returning a large amount of content (reading a large file, many search results), and complex multi-step tasks. To trigger it less often, open a new thread once a topic is done rather than keeping an old thread alive, keep prompts concise, and avoid pasting large repeated blocks; the /compact command triggers compression deliberately. Levels Compression escalates from gentle to aggressive only when necessary: | Level | Strategy | Degree of loss | | --- | --- | --- | | Level 1 | Remove intermediate tool results | Very low; tool results can be fetched again | | Level 2 | Summarize historical messages | Medium; keeps semantics, loses detail | | Level 3 | Remove earlier conversation rounds | Higher; keeps only the most recent content | | Level 4 | Keep only the core setup and the current request | Very high; emergency degradation | What is protected Without compression, a long conversation ends in one of three ways: an outright error, a brute-force truncation, or manual control of conversation length. Compression is a system capability, so conversation length needs no manual management. Compression protects three things first: the continuity of the conversation, so it is not interrupted for being too long; the facts genuinely needed, favoring information useful to the current task; and traceability, so every compression leaves a record of what it compressed and what it kept for administrators to inspect. There are two bottom lines. First, compression can only trim and reorganize existing content; it never invents. Second, a thread's core setup (the system prompt) is frozen at creation, and compression acts only on the conversation history and tool results, so an agent never "forgets who it is" because of compression. Compression records Every compression leaves a record that includes the strategy used, the context size before and after, and a rough assessment of the information lost. Administrators use it to judge whether compression has affected task quality. Local reduction When automatic compression triggers, the system first sees whether earlier file reads, searches, and listing results can be shortened. The last 5 groups of tool results, error information, media, and results that still need pagination are protected. A shortened old result still carries its location, a head/tail preview, and an explicit omission notice, so the agent can read it again when needed. If the local reduction has already freed enough space, no extra model call is made to produce a summary; if not, the summary flow runs. Manual compression and overflow recovery go straight to summarization. A summary outputs at most 2048 tokens by default, and if the model itself is configured with a smaller output limit, the smaller one wins. Administrators can see the estimated savings of the local reduction in the progress records. The estimate is for diagnosis only; actual token consumption follows the model provider's report. Limits After compression, the system favors what the current task needs. Only in extreme cases (a very long conversation stacked with a large amount of tool output) might the agent recall early details less precisely, and then a new conversation thread is the fix. Triggers Levels What is protected Compression records Local reduction Limits

title: Subagents
summary: The 11 actions of Subagent Control, the `user_round` + `model_round` parent–child round references, and the removal of swarm orchestration from the engine and protocol layer.
text: Subagents The 11 actions of Subagent Control, the userround + modelround parent–child round references, and the removal of swarm orchestration from the engine and protocol layer. # Subagents The parent thread hands one subtask to an independent executor, which runs it and passes the result back to the parent thread. Control actions 子智能体控制 (Subagent Control) provides 11 actions: | Action | Action | Action | | --- | --- | --- | | spawn | batchspawn | wait | | interrupt | close | resume | | report | send | status | | list | history | | Parent–child round references are encoded as userround + modelround, and an executor's rounds hang under that pair of parent round references. The sub-session's user message is hidden, and it wakes with auto-wake. Limits The only collaborative form is the subagent. Swarm orchestration (swarm tools, hives, orchestration mode, team runs, swarm packs) has been removed from the engine and the protocol layer; it is not waiting to be implemented, nor hidden behind a switch. Swarm leftovers remain in TUI prompts, front-end i18n labels, and compatibility shims; the empty directories have been deleted. Those leftovers do not mean the capability exists. Subagents Control actions Limits

title: Scheduled Tasks
summary: The semantics and bounds of the at, every, and cron schedule kinds, the two delivery targets, lease, backoff, and auto-disable parameters, and support by form.
headings: Entry points and support by form
text: Scheduled Tasks The semantics and bounds of the at, every, and cron schedule kinds, the two delivery targets, lease, backoff, and auto-disable parameters, and support by form. The task definition is persisted in storage, and a background loop claims work by due time, independent of which session you happen to be viewing. Every run is recorded (/wunder/cron/runs): whether it ran, whether it succeeded, and when it will run next; failures come with backoff and auto-disable; and a process restart does not lose the task definitions. This differs from waiting inside a session: a scheduled task creates a new run in the future and does not occupy the current thread's turn. Scheduled tasks diagram: scheduling rules enter the scheduler, then dispatch to background execution and execution records Schedule kinds The kind field is one of at, every, or cron. | Kind | Semantics | Input | Bounds | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | at | One-off point in time | An RFC3339 timestamp | At most 365 days ahead; auto-disabled once it runs (disabled with a reason if it fails) | | every | Fixed interval | everyms (optional start time) | 1,000 ms ≤ interval ≤ 86,400,000 ms (24 hours) | | cron | Recurring expression | A 5–7 field expression plus an optional timezone | Fields accept only digits and / - , ?; the timezone is parsed as a named timezone, defaulting to the local timezone | Natural language also works in tools and quick input, and the system converts it into the kinds above: every 5 minutes becomes a fixed interval, and daily at 9am and weekdays at 6pm become the corresponding cron expressions; when it cannot parse the input, it suggests the formats that are accepted. Content limits: a task name is at most 128 characters, and a trigger message at most 16,384 characters. Result delivery sessiontarget has two values. | Value | Behavior | | --- | --- | | main (default) | The result is delivered to the bound current session, continuing the same conversation | | isolated | Each run creates a separate thread session and keeps a link back to the parent session | Choose isolated for recurring tasks that need a trail and should not disturb the main conversation; choose main when you want the result appended directly to the existing context. Execution guarantees In multi-instance deployments a lease prevents duplicate execution: when a task is claimed, the runner's identity, a run token, and a lease expiry are written, and the lease is renewed with a heartbeat while the run lasts; if the process crashes, the lease expires and another instance can claim the task. Each record also carries a deduplication key and a consecutive-failure count, and writes down why it was disabled. Default scheduling parameters: | Parameter | Default | | --- | --- | | Max concurrent runs | 1 | | Poll interval | 1000 ms | | Max idle sleep | 5000 ms | | Lease lifetime / heartbeat | 300 seconds / 60 seconds | | Consecutive-failure auto-disable threshold | 5 | After a failure, backoff steps up with the consecutive-failure count: 30 seconds → 60 seconds → 5 minutes → 15 minutes → 1 hour, then stays at the last step. Once the failure limit is reached, the task is auto-disabled with a written reason; re-enabling it resets the failure count. Master switch With the master switch off (cron.enabled=false), four kinds of write operation are rejected: add, update, enable, and run, each with a clear message. Status, list, a single detail, run records, delete, and disable all remain available, so existing tasks can still be reviewed and cleaned up. Entry points and support by form | Surface | Status | | --- | --- | | API | /wunder/cron/, 12 endpoints in all (status / list / workspaces / runs / add / update / remove / enable / disable / get / run / action), on the user side, isolated by user ownership | | Tool | The built-in scheduled-tasks tool (canonical name 定时任务, alias scheduletask), sharing the same handler as the API, so the model can create tasks on its own | | Cloud | A scheduled-tasks category page under settings | | Desktop | A scheduled-tasks page plus a native entry point, calling the same handler in-process | | CLI | No scheduled tasks: the local engine explicitly disables the scheduler at startup, and there is no related slash command | | Admin | No user-level task management page; it exists only as a template configuration under preset agents | When you need something to run on a schedule, configure it on the Cloud, the Desktop, or the Server side. Schedule kinds Result delivery Execution guarantees Master switch Entry points and support by form

title: Channels
summary: The support level of Feishu, QQ, WeChat, XMPP, and generic webhooks; the binding score that routes a message to its agent and workspace; inbound, outbound, and rate-limit parameters.
text: Channels The support level of Feishu, QQ, WeChat, XMPP, and generic webhooks; the binding score that routes a message to its agent and workspace; inbound, outbound, and rate-limit parameters. ## Scope of responsibility All execution happens in the engine. A channel does just two things: parse an external message into a unified inbound shape, and deliver the unified outbound shape back into an external protocol. Protocol adaptation stops at the entry; a channel does not copy business logic, does not keep its own storage, and does not change thread semantics. The same task thread can take a message from Cloud, continue it from Feishu, and finish it from Desktop; a channel never creates a second execution path. A form (Desktop / Cloud / CLI / Server) is the shape of running and access; a channel (Feishu / QQ / WeChat …) is an off-site platform. The two are not one layer. The statement that many entries share one engine holds; what tends to be written wrong is the support level. Support level Feishu (feishu): a persistent connection plus a webhook, fully implemented, with a dedicated webhook entry point. QQ Bot (qqbot): a persistent connection plus a webhook, fully implemented, with a dedicated webhook entry point. WeChat (weixin): runs on a persistent connection (iLink long polling), fully implemented, and the largest in scale. XMPP (xmpp): a persistent connection plus a webhook. It is disabled by default and is only a placeholder then, returning a "not enabled" notice for all send and receive; it becomes a real implementation only once explicitly turned on. WeCom (wechat): webhook only, partially implemented (send, receive, and signature verification), with no persistent connection. WeChat Official Account (wechatmp): webhook only, partially implemented, with no persistent connection. WhatsApp Cloud (whatsappcloud): webhook only, partially implemented, with no persistent connection. Only four channels use a persistent connection: Feishu, QQ Bot, XMPP, and WeChat (weixin). WeCom, the Official Account, and WhatsApp Cloud are pure webhook callbacks. The following platforms have no adapter at all: telegram, discord, slack, LINE, DingTalk. They exist only as generic-webhook directory entries, handled through the generic entry point and generic parsing — with no platform-specific signature verification, rich-text mapping, attachment download, or proactive push. The accurate statement is that they are visible in the directory and can send and receive text over a generic webhook, but they have no platform-specific adapter. Writing them up as "supported channels" is wrong. Binding resolution An inbound message is first resolved by binding: candidates are scored by specificity, the single best one is taken, and priority breaks a tie. | Dimension | Score | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Exact peerid match | 8 | Supports the wildcard, and a wildcard scores nothing | | peerkind match | 4 | dm/direct/single/user are treated as the same kind | | accountid match | 2 | Empty means wildcard | | channel match | 1 | Empty means wildcard | A hit yields the target agent and any tool overrides, after which the workspace is decided: empty, as well as the default and default aliases, all point to that user's default agent workspace. In the Server form, workspaces are flattened per user into a single cloud directory, so files arriving from different channels for the same user land in the same place. Inbound, outbound, and rate limiting Inbound uses a bounded queue: capacity 512, concurrency 8, enqueue timeout 80 ms. A full queue or an enqueue timeout counts as backpressure and reports "queue busy" rather than piling up without limit. The visible effect is that the platform redelivers or briefly delays; messages are not silently dropped. Outbound runs on a persistent queue with exponential backoff, defaulting to a 500 ms polling interval, batches of 50, and at most 5 retries, with a backoff base of 2 s and a ceiling of 60 s. Outbound delivery has a switch. When it is off, delivery is instead attempted once synchronously at enqueue time and is no longer redelivered by the polling loop. When troubleshooting a "received but no reply" case, check this switch first: once it is off and that one synchronous attempt fails, the message sits in the outbound queue waiting for manual handling. Rate limiting is a token bucket of QPS plus a concurrency cap per channel account; both at 0 means no limiting. A rate-limited request does not consume a concurrency slot and is handed to the outbound queue for backoff redelivery. Attachments and media Inbound media is downloaded, transcoded, and dropped into the workspace for that channel before being handed to the engine; platform-specific files have their own download entry points and likewise write into the workspace; and a further kind of pending file is reserved first and fetched on demand. Outbound attachments are extracted from the body, from Markdown, or from a workspace path and then uploaded. Channel clients usually do not understand internal paths, so attachments go out as an upload link rather than a path string thrown at the user. Webhook entry points and verification The generic entry point is POST /wunder/channel/{provider}/webhook; Feishu and QQ Bot have their own dedicated entry points at POST /wunder/channel/feishu/webhook and POST /wunder/channel/qqbot/webhook. Verification differs by platform: some loop back a verification token from configuration, some use a content signature, and WeCom additionally verifies the signature and decrypts the encrypted message. The generic webhook does no platform-specific verification, so platforms that use the generic entry point need to close this off themselves at a gateway or reverse proxy to guarantee a trustworthy source. Troubleshooting messages 1. Presence: for a persistent-connection channel, check whether its connection process is running; a webhook-only channel has no notion of presence, so check only whether the callback arrives. 2. Whether the callback arrives: check the platform-side push logs and the channel's runtime logs. 3. Whether it was routed: check the binding score and the enabled state; a binding to a different agent looks exactly like no response at all. 4. Arrived but no reply: check for records stuck in the outbound queue, whether the outbound delivery loop is off, and whether rate limiting was hit. 5. XMPP specifics: confirm whether it is enabled — while disabled by default it is only a placeholder, and errors say so directly. Points not to mix up telegram / discord / slack / LINE / DingTalk have no adapter; they are only generic directory entries. WeCom and the Official Account have no persistent connection; only Feishu, QQ Bot, XMPP, and WeChat have one. XMPP is disabled by default, and while disabled it is a placeholder. A channel cannot be configured with business logic; it has only two layers, the target agent and tool overrides, and everything else lives in the engine and on the management side. The core capabilities are the same across channels; the differences are only in protocol expression (rich text, attachments, cards) and whether a persistent connection is supported. The inbound queue does not guarantee no loss by queuing forever; it is bounded at 512 with an 80 ms enqueue timeout, and anything beyond goes to backpressure and platform redelivery. A failed outbound delivery is not dropped outright; it uses a persistent queue with exponential backoff and at most 5 retries. Desktop and CLI do not go through the channel layer: Desktop is a native in-process call, and CLI uses its own access path. Scope of responsibility Support level Binding resolution Inbound, outbound, and rate limiting Attachments and media Webhook entry points and verification Troubleshooting messages Points not to mix up

title: Memory
summary: Long-term material injected once as an index at thread creation and then frozen, the three fragment layers (L0/L1/L2) with core/working/peripheral tiers, and how memory divides the work with the workspace and the knowledge base.
text: Memory Long-term material injected once as an index at thread creation and then frozen, the three fragment layers (L0/L1/L2) with core/working/peripheral tiers, and how memory divides the work with the workspace and the knowledge base. An agent needs long-term information — who the user is, what they prefer, what policies an organization has, what background a project has. Such material is injected once when the thread is created and stays frozen afterwards, never rewritten dynamically on every round. Three things follow: cognitive boundaries stay stable while the thread runs, so it does not drift as the conversation goes on; the system prompt stays stable, which helps cache acceleration; and it can clearly answer what background this thread started from. On the user side this shows up as personal preferences taking effect automatically in new conversations and the agent being able to use long-term material in the workspace and knowledge base. On the administrator side it shows up as controllable injection rules, sensitive information not leaking, conversations of the same kind starting from the same background, and a thread's initialization background being traceable. Layered structure Fragments are split into three layers by injection cost: L0 title (titlel0, the only body text injected into the system prompt), L1 summary (summaryl1, shown in lists and search hits), and L2 content (contentl2, returned only by get). Fragments also carry a tier: core / working / peripheral (new fragments default to working). The tier affects ranking and retention weight, but never changes the "L0 index only" injection shape. When a thread is created, the system writes the L0 index into the system prompt as the thread's cognitive base; the body text is pulled on demand through the memory-management tool (list / search / get / add / update / remove / clear). Semantic recall is currently disabled (inventory mode); recall is only an alias of search, not a separate channel. Structure Memory uses structured fragments rather than one long free-text block. Fragments are found by lookup, replaced individually without affecting the rest, marked invalid when outdated (superseded / invalidated), and carry traceable version relationships (supersedesmemoryid / supersededbymemoryid). Freezing rules Once the system prompt is set it stays frozen, and later conversation never modifies it dynamically, which keeps thread behavior stable. Long-term memory is injected only once at thread creation; even if search (or the recall alias) fires during a run, its result is only supplementary reference and never rewrites the system prompt. Division of sources Workspaces, knowledge bases, and memory can all supply material, but their responsibilities differ: | Source | Character | Use | | --- | --- | --- | | Workspace | The scene of the current task | Holds the files being worked on | | Knowledge base | A long-term document source | Retrieves policies, material, and reference documents | | Memory | Structured accumulation | Remembers who the user is, their preferences, and past decisions | When updates take effect When a memory update takes effect depends on the thread: a newly created thread applies the latest memory automatically, while an existing thread is unaffected and keeps the copy from when it was created. After a personal preference is updated, a new conversation is needed for it to take effect. Limits Memory and context compression have different jobs: compression governs near-field information such as conversation history, while memory supplies far-field information such as long-term background. Compression does not touch the memory inside the system prompt. More memory is not better. Injecting too much crowds the conversation's context space, introduces irrelevant information that disturbs judgment, and raises token consumption. The system therefore has selection and limiting mechanisms and does not inject without bound. Points not to mix up Memory does not update automatically every round; it is injected only at initialization and does not change during a run. Retrieval through the memory-management tool is a dynamic supplement and does not rewrite the base. Workspace files are not the same as memory either — a workspace is the scene of the current task, while memory is long-term accumulation. Layered structure Structure Freezing rules Division of sources When updates take effect Limits Points not to mix up

title: Multi-threading
summary: Scheduling, locks, and realtime state isolated per thread inside one process: the Desktop frontend's local waiting queue and the Cloud engine session queue, a 120-second session lock TTL, tool parallelism ≤ 4, and a round cap of 1000.
text: Multi-threading Scheduling, locks, and realtime state isolated per thread inside one process: the Desktop frontend's local waiting queue and the Cloud engine session queue, a 120-second session lock TTL, tool parallelism ≤ 4, and a round cap of 1000. # Multi-threading A single user can hold several task threads at once, and scheduling, locks, and realtime state are isolated per thread so the threads do not block one another. Concurrency control Queueing has two layers: since Desktop v1.0.0 the frontend local waiting queue (waitingturns) holds messages sent during a run above the input box and sends them when the current turn settles; the Cloud build still uses the engine-level session queue (on by default, in-order execution). A session lock has a TTL of 120 seconds with heartbeat renewal; when its holder exits abnormally, the TTL releases it. Tool parallelism ≤ 4: tools that run in parallel take a read lock, and tools that run exclusively take a write lock. Round caps, active-session caps, daily quotas, and retry circuit breaking form four hard constraints. Defaults | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Session lock TTL | 120 seconds (with heartbeat) | | Tool parallelism | ≤ 4 | | Round cap | 1000 by default | Limits With agentqueue.enabled turned off, the Cloud build judges a message sent during a run as "user busy" and no longer shows it in the queue bar (the Server warns about this at startup). This is a configuration choice, not a fault; the Desktop build is unaffected and uses the frontend local waiting queue. Blocking category quotas and bounded queues are hard caps: when full, the system reports busy and does not wait in a queue. Multi-threading Concurrency control Defaults Limits

title: Multi-user Management
summary: Users, units, and permission boundaries in the Server form — opaque tokens, presence split by form, the unit tree, levels and credits, worker cards, and data isolation.
text: Multi-user Management Users, units, and permission boundaries in the Server form — opaque tokens, presence split by form, the unit tree, levels and credits, worker cards, and data isolation. Multi-user governance is a foundational capability of the Server form; the Desktop, Android, and the CLI are local, single-machine forms with no account system. Concrete panel operations are covered in the reference section. Identity checks Management gate: management paths (such as /wunder/admin/) require an API key or a Bearer token on the server side, and the account must be an administrator; a unit head is separately allowed on designated paths. User ownership: a user-facing request is first resolved to a user by Bearer, then its ownership is checked, ensuring it can touch only its own sessions, tools, and tasks. Realtime channels: a WebSocket connection carries a token in its handshake, and each of the six realtime channels authenticates on its own. Tokens | Credential | Shape | Default lifetime | | --- | --- | --- | | Access token | A random string starting with wund, verified by looking it up in the database | 7 days | | Refresh token | A random string starting with wundr | 30 days | | External-login one-time code | Starting with wundc, held in memory | Short-lived | A token is not a self-contained JWT: it carries no claims and cannot be parsed offline. Validation is a database lookup, so revocation takes effect immediately. A few key semantics: Refresh is an OAuth-style family rotation: one refresh issues a new access plus a new refresh, both in the same rotation family; presenting an already-revoked token to refresh again is judged to be a stolen token, and the whole family (including the access token in use) is revoked at once. The session scope decides who can renew: login reads the x-wunder-session-scope header, and only local scopes such as the Desktop and the CLI get a refresh chain that can renew; browser sessions do not take this path. Logging in again from the same scope evicts the old session: when the same user logs in again from the same scope, the old session receives a notice that it has been superseded and is disconnected. When troubleshooting a connection that dropped on another client, first check whether it was the same scope logging in again. Passwords are stored as Argon2 hashes; plaintext never reaches the database. Presence Presence is recorded separately by client type, with the Cloud (web), the Desktop, and the CLI as three independent lines; roughly 90 seconds without a touch counts as offline, with a sweep interval of 30 seconds (minimum 10 seconds). As a result, presence in the user list is split into web, desktop, and cli columns — "online" is no longer a yes-or-no value, and to see who is online on which form you look at the matching column. The management exit is at /wunder/admin/gateway/presence. Unit tree At startup, if the unit table is empty, it is automatically seeded from a unit template. The unit tree is at most 4 levels deep. The unit-head role is allowed only on the two paths /wunder/admin/orgunits and /wunder/admin/useraccounts; its data scope equals the units it heads plus their descendant units, and stepping outside that scope is a permission denial. The frontend's check is only a convenience; the unit-head boundary is ultimately enforced by the server. Levels and credits Levels lean toward growth display: XP equals the integer number of seconds the session has run, the level cap is 200 (MAXUSERLEVEL), and the XP needed to reach the next level increases as 240 + 28L + 0.9L². Levels unlock no resource; they only reflect time spent. Credits lean toward governance: every user holds an integer Credits account with a balance, cumulative issuance, cumulative consumption, and a daily grant (1000 per day by default). It is an abstract allowance of issuance and deduction, not a token count — each request sent to the model service deducts exactly 1 Credit, independent of token metering. When the balance is short, a new request is rejected by quota and returns a snapshot of the remaining allowance; administrator accounts are exempt from deduction but still record request counts. Worker cards and threads | Concept | What it is | | --- | --- | | worker card (.worker-card.json) | An agent's portable definition document, holding basic information (identifier, name, description, icon), prompts, capabilities, interaction, runtime settings, and preset publication status | | Thread / session | The continuous unit of execution once an agent is invoked; one agent can hold several independent task threads at once | Sessions bind to an agent by agent id, and their task threads stay independent of one another. After a preset agent is published, you can control which units can see it and decide which fields a bound user may change. Note that the disk directory for preset cards (useragents.workercardsroot) is an empty string by default — without explicit configuration there is no preset card loaded from disk, so this capability does not ship out of the box. Approval mode has three values, suggest, autoedit, and fullauto, with fullauto the default. Data isolation Sessions, tasks, workspaces, tools, and channel bindings are all isolated by user ownership, and the user-facing side checks ownership handler by handler. Cloud files and execution boundaries are carried by a sandbox: read-write and execute operations run in each user's own container, mounting only that user's own directory, and path checking is no longer responsible for tenant isolation. Quotas, levels, and presence are account-level; model configuration and preset agents are unit-level or global-level. Points not to mix up A token is not a self-contained JWT and cannot be parsed offline — it is an opaque random string, verified by a database lookup, and revocation takes effect immediately. A lost refresh cannot be replaced by resending the old one; replaying an old refresh triggers whole-family revocation, and the correct move is to log in again. Credits are not a token budget; they are an integer request allowance, one deduction per model request, with token usage metered separately. A unit head cannot manage every admin page; it is allowed only on the unit and user-account paths, and only within descendant units. A worker card is not a task thread; it is an agent's definition document, while a thread is a unit of execution — two different layers. The system does not ship a set of preset agent cards; the preset card directory is empty by default, and nothing exists until it is configured. Identity checks Tokens Presence Unit tree Levels and credits Worker cards and threads Data isolation Points not to mix up

title: Compatibility
summary: Offline build chains, software rendering, and terminal adaptation for the Desktop and the CLI on Windows 7 32-bit and Ubuntu 18.04.
text: Compatibility Offline build chains, software rendering, and terminal adaptation for the Desktop and the CLI on Windows 7 32-bit and Ubuntu 18.04. # Compatibility Supported systems | System | Approach | | --- | --- | | Windows 7, 32-bit | A dedicated i686-win7-windows-gnu Tier 3 target plus a build-std offline toolchain | | Ubuntu 18.04 x64 / arm64 | An offline build chain and sysroot | Runtime constraints The interface does not depend on a GPU: Slint uses software rendering. Building does not depend on network access: both the Windows 7 32-bit and the Ubuntu 18.04 chains are offline toolchains, and the Ubuntu side carries a sysroot as well. Command sessions adapt to old terminals: command sessions are carried over winpty, and output is decoded as GBK. Startup checks: a recovery scan and self-check run at startup. Both chains work offline, the interface needs no GPU, and command sessions adapt to legacy terminals — Windows 7 32-bit and Ubuntu 18.04 (x64 / arm64) can run the Desktop and the CLI directly. Limits Build scripts still carry dead Tauri links, pointing at directories that no longer exist. That is an engineering gap, not a capability. win7 interlink nodes do not declare tool.exec, so the capability surface on legacy devices is narrower. Compatibility Supported systems Runtime constraints Limits

title: Agent Loop
summary: The model-round granularity of the main loop, round and tool-call budgets, circuit-breaking and timeout guardrails, and the frozen system prompt of a thread.
text: Agent Loop The model-round granularity of the main loop, round and tool-call budgets, circuit-breaking and timeout guardrails, and the frozen system prompt of a thread. The engine calls the model repeatedly to advance a task, and each model call can carry a batch of tool executions, until it produces a deliverable result or hits a brake. The goal is stated once; the steps in between need no steering. Main loop Each model round does three things: it checks whether it should yield and whether the round cap has been exceeded, compressing the context when necessary; it calls the model and gets back a piece of text or a batch of tool calls; and it runs those tool calls in parallel or exclusively, writing the results back into the history as observations before moving to the next round. When there are no tool calls, or a brake is hit, the round lands and the loop exits. The granularity follows Sessions and Rounds: One model round is one model call by the engine. A single round can contain several tool calls, and tool calls are not counted as separate rounds. Each round corresponds to one visible output in the interface; a tool batch is a separate entry in the timeline but is not a separate round. Guardrails Model round cap: non-administrator accounts default to at most 1000 rounds, and it stops once they are used up. Per-round tool-call budget: at most 10000 tool calls in a round; memory recall 2000 and library-query calls 2000 (relaxable to 10000 when necessary), and calls of a type beyond its limit are rejected. Repeated-failure circuit breaker: it stops when the same failure fingerprint recurs — 5 times for non-retryable errors, 2 times for parameter or protocol errors, and 4 times for "succeeded without progress"; after stopping it relays the failure reason to you. Context-overflow self-healing: at most 8 recovery attempts, each doing a corrective compression first and then retrying. Empty-output protection: one automatic retry (resampling with reasoning effort turned off); if it is still empty, it errors out and stops. Timeouts: model and tools default to 120 s each, with an additional idle watchdog; a timeout counts as a failure toward the circuit breaker. Session lock: the same thread runs serially, with a lock TTL of 120 s and a 5 s heartbeat; if the holder exits abnormally, the TTL releases it. Active-session cap: non-administrators are limited to 300, and beyond that requests queue or are told to try again later. Tool parallelism: at most 4; read-only tools run in parallel and exclusive tools run serially. Approval and risk tiering are independent of the loop: write or execute calls suspend and wait for your decision, and approval results are cached by tool category for 600 s so the same kind of operation is not asked about again and again. Terminal states Every round of the loop must finally land on a result, which the interface state reflects: Completed normally: a deliverable reply is produced. Rejected: the request was not admitted (busy, quota exhausted, invalid request). Cancelled: you stopped it yourself. Failed: the execution errored (tool guardrail, no-progress guard, model error). While it waits for your input or for an approval, the thread is not in a terminal state; it is still within its lifetime. Threads An agent can hold several independent task threads at once; scheduling, locking, and realtime state are all isolated per thread, and different threads do not block one another. Once a thread is set, the system prompt is frozen and long-term memory is injected only once at initialization and never rewritten afterwards. This keeps long tasks behaviorally stable and lets the model-side cache be reused. A subagent is a unit of work the main agent creates on the fly; it runs its own loop, passes results back to the parent thread, and is reclaimed when the task ends. This is the only form of collaboration. Intervention An approval pops up, so approve or reject it, and the thread continues. The inquiry panel asks, and the thread moves to waiting for human input; after you add an instruction, the new user round carries the new context. Seeing "running tool" or several tool entries appearing one after another means the loop is advancing. Sending the same sentence again does not speed it up; it only queues another user round. There has been no output for a long time while the state is still running, so stop the thread and restate the goal. Open a new thread when the topic changes, the context is already very long, or you need a clean prompt base: after an agent's setup or its memory is changed, only a new thread picks it up. Points not to mix up The claim that every tool call counts as a round is wrong — a tool batch belongs to the same model round. The loop does not retry without limit; repeated failures, progress-free successes, overruns, and empty output all have circuit breakers. A still interface does not mean the loop has stopped; waiting for approval, waiting for input, and queued are all still within the lifetime. Streaming output is only a way of presenting things; the truth of the loop is in the thread ledger. A subagent does not share the parent thread's context; it is an independent thread with an independent loop, interacting only through callbacks and a mailbox. Main loop Guardrails Terminal states Threads Intervention Points not to mix up

title: Tools
summary: How the four layers — tools, skills, capabilities, and user tools — are told apart, canonical names and aliases, dispatch order for dynamic registration, default sets and visibility gates, and the two result-trimming tracks.
text: Tools How the four layers — tools, skills, capabilities, and user tools — are told apart, canonical names and aliases, dispatch order for dynamic registration, default sets and visibility gates, and the two result-trimming tracks. The agent's ability to act is collectively called "tools," but tools, skills, capabilities, and user tools are four different layers, and conflating them is the most common cause of broken configuration.
