Tools layer diagram: tool description, execution layer, model input results, and display projection—four related layers The four layers | Layer | What it is | Who uses it | How to tell | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Tool | Executor: one call reads a file, runs a command, or sends a request | The model calls it directly; the engine dispatches and runs it | Registered in the tool catalog and carries a dispatch branch | | Skill | Knowledge-and-script package: a directory holding the SKILL.md body and an entry script | The model can call it by skill name, or read the body through the skill-call action | Registered in the skill catalog | | Capability | Selection unit on the governance side: a unified descriptor an administrator uses to choose what an agent may use | Configured on the admin side; never enters the execution chain | Its source is built-in, MCP, skill, knowledge base, user MCP, user skill, user knowledge base, or shared | | User tool | An extension the user connects, in three kinds: MCP, skill, knowledge base | Mounted per user; the alias enters the routing table | Registered in the user tool catalog | A capability being selected does not mean an executor exists, and an executor existing does not mean the model can see it. Canonical names and aliases Most of the tool names the model sees are Chinese canonical names, with English aliases alongside, and a normalization pass runs before every invocation. | Canonical | Common aliases | Canonical | Common aliases | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 执行命令 | executecommand | 读取文件 | readfile | | 命令会话 | commandsession, writecommandstdin | 写入文件 | writefile | | 网页搜索 | websearch | 文本编辑 | edit, patch, applypatch, 应用补丁 | | 列出文件 | listfiles | 搜索内容 | searchcontent | | 文件名匹配 | glob | 技能调用 | skillcall, skillget | | 计划面板 | updateplan | 问询面板 | questionpanel, askpanel | | 定时任务 | scheduletask | 记忆管理 | memorymanager, memorymanage | | 子智能体控制 | subagentcontrol | 网页抓取 | webfetch | When a tool is written down in configuration, logs, or documentation, give both the canonical name and the alias; writing only one makes the two easy to mismatch. Dynamic registration The names that enter the model's tool list are assembled from four kinds of dynamic registration. | Source | Name on the model side | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | MCP server | server@tool | Registered tool by tool; on a name clash the display name gains a server-name or hash suffix | | Packed MCP | server@mcppack | A server marked as packed folds into a single tool whose actions are list, get, and call | | Skill | The skill name itself | A skill name can be called directly; the skill-call action reads the body and substitutes the skill root-path placeholder | | Knowledge base | The knowledge base name | Registered one base at a time, replacing the old single knowledge tool | | User-tool alias | The alias | Dispatch routes by alias first; a hit goes straight to the user tool | Dispatch order is alias → skill → MCP → knowledge base → built-in tools, and a hit earlier in the chain short-circuits the rest. Default sets and per-form differences Default tool sets, the desktop hidden set, and the desktop extra set all have a single registration; do not keep a second copy in the docs or the configuration. | Set | Contents | | --- | --- | | Default built-ins (12) | 定时任务, 记忆管理, 执行命令, 命令会话, 列出文件, 文件名匹配, 搜索内容, 读取文件, 网页抓取, 技能调用, 写入文件, 文本编辑 | | Default skills | 技能创建器, 公文写作, 文稿校对, 3D网页, 知识短片 | | Desktop hidden (neither selectable nor on by default) | goal (action=get|edit|pause|resume|complete|blocked, injected automatically by the runtime per session; the model cannot create goals), 会话线程控制 | | Desktop extras, on by default | 读图工具, 桌面控制, 子智能体控制 | 网页搜索 is temporarily withdrawn, not deleted: the code is kept and dispatch still recognizes it, but the availability check returns unavailable, so neither the model nor the user can see it. ptc has been removed entirely. Visibility also runs through a few real gates. | Gate | Effect | | --- | --- | | The model has no vision | Filters out 读图工具 and the desktop tools | | The matching model or service is not configured | Speech generation, speech-to-text, image generation, and video generation each go unavailable | | Configuration not enabled | 网页抓取, 网页搜索, browser, and the desktop tools | | Form | The desktop form filters out the hidden set | Browser is one strict tool: once enabled the model calls browser(action=...), and each action exposes only its required fields. The aggregate display name "Browser" represents that same capability. Result trimming Display trimming and model-input trimming are separate and do not affect each other. | Track | Rule | Affects | | --- | --- | --- | | Display | A preview of at most 2,400 characters or 16 lines, with an ellipsis past that | Only the client display; the raw result is kept in full and can be copied | | Model input | Trimmed by budget, with reproducible old observations compressed | What the model sees at the next step | Seeing "…" in the UI does not mean the model sees that same truncated copy; and when the model's context has been compressed to a preview, the UI may still show the full content. To judge context pressure, look at the compression page and the usage page, not the collapsing in the UI. Approval tiers Approvals are filed by the tool's risk category, and there are four categories: read-only, file write, running a command or a script, and controlling host capabilities. Pending requests are registered in two kinds by source: chat connection and channel. The cache that lets one approval cover a short window lasts 600 seconds within the same session. Execution policy has three states: allow, audit, and enforce; under enforce, high-risk actions must have human approval. A front-end confirmation cannot replace back-end authorization. The four layers Canonical names and aliases Dynamic registration Default sets and per-form differences Result trimming Approval tiers

title: Tool System
summary: The path a tool call takes from parsing, orchestration, and dispatch to persistence, reasons a tool is invisible, naming and registration, parallelism, timeouts, budgets, clipping, and MCP integration.
text: Tool System The path a tool call takes from parsing, orchestration, and dispatch to persistence, reasons a tool is invisible, naming and registration, parallelism, timeouts, budgets, clipping, and MCP integration. Layered concepts, the default set, and naming conventions live in Tools (core concepts), and per-tool usage is in the Tools overview. Call Path Two points are easy to get wrong: The four stages "pre → execute → post → result" only describe the model; hooks are off by default and are not the main execution chain. A business failure is not raised as an error in the dispatch layer but returned as a normal path. "The tool returned but the business did not succeed" is normal, and the model reads the reason for the failure. Why a Tool Is Invisible | Where it is stuck | Criterion | | --- | --- | | Not registered | The name is not in the canonical-name / alias table, and no matching MCP, skill, or knowledge base exists | | Temporarily withdrawn | Web search: the code is still there but it is invisible in every case | | Not in the capability selection layer | The administrator has not selected that capability for this agent | | Filtered by form | Desktop mode hides target-management actions and session thread control | | Filtered by a capability threshold | Without vision, image reading and desktop tools are filtered out; the multimodal set needs a matching model; web fetching / browser need configuration enabled first | | Name short-circuited | When an alias and a skill share a name, the earlier route matches first | Naming and Dynamic Registration MCP tools are named "server @ tool"; a package-enabled server folds into a single tool operated through three actions: list, get detail, and call. When a tool name collides across servers, a server-name segment is appended; a collision within one server adds a runtime suffix. A skill name can be called directly; a knowledge base is registered library by library, and there is no single "knowledge base" tool. A user-defined tool alias enters the alias table and is routed by alias first during dispatch. Parallelism, Timeouts, and Budgets | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Parallelism ceiling | 4 | | Parallel decision | Whether a batch of tool calls can run in parallel is decided in the orchestration layer | | Lock semantics | A parallelizable tool takes a read lock; an exclusive tool takes a write lock | | Default tool timeout | 120 seconds (minimum 1 second) | | Tool-call budget | 10000 per round | | Memory-recall budget | 2000 per round | Tools outside the parallelism allowlist run serially, deliberately: write and execution tools are exclusive. Two Clipping Channels for Results | Channel | Behavior | Impact | | --- | --- | --- | | Display | Preview 2400 characters and 16 lines, with an ellipsis beyond that | Affects client rendering only; the original message and copied content stay complete | | Model input | Truncate head and tail by budget; older history is summarized by full compaction | Decides what the model sees next | The budget into the model: 10000 characters at each of head and tail; arrays at most 128 items (48 head + 16 tail); paged results 500 items (180 head + 60 tail). Clipping adds a "truncated" marker, so the model can see that content was cut. Full-compaction conventions: the summary model produces the replacement history; standalone micro-compaction has been removed, so there is no more "most recent 5 groups / 768-byte preview" clipping. MCP Integration An external MCP client must be configured with a name, endpoint, transport, request headers, authentication, allowed tools, whether to package, and tool specs. The Server's built-in MCP service endpoint is /wunder/mcp (streamable-http), exposing two tools, wunder@excute and doc2md; it returns 501 when the matching capability is off. The standalone Python FastMCP service carries its own configuration and toolset and is not part of this engine. Protocol and Provider The tool-call protocol is decided by the provider: | Situation | Mode | | --- | --- | | The model explicitly configures a tool-call mode | Follow the configuration | | The provider is openai | Text-protocol tool calls | | Any other provider | Native function calls | | An unrecognized value | Fall back to the tag / xml text protocol | The text protocol's lark syntax is currently reserved for the patch form of text editing; parameter repair and nested restoration happen in the core library. There is no separate tool-protocol branch for Win7; the confirmed difference is only on the interop side — an older Win7 node does not declare the "execute command" capability. Removed and Merged | Status | Item | | --- | --- | | Removed | ptc, user-world tools, channel tools, a2a tools, finalresponse, a2ui tools, LSP query / node-call tools, the standalone sleep-and-wait tool, and session yield | | Merged | applypatch merged into text editing (one tool with three forms: replace / patch / subcommand) | | Temporarily withdrawn | Web search (code kept, invisible) | Limits The four-stage model is not the main execution chain, and hooks are off by default. A clipped result does not mean the model cannot see it: the display channel and the model input channel are separate. More tools do not mean better selection; many names and vague descriptions raise the error rate, so the default set is deliberately restrained. A tool error is not a failed call: a business failure is returned to the model as a normal result with a reason and a next-step hint. Only reads on the parallelism allowlist can run in parallel; writes and executions are exclusive. Win7 has no tool-protocol fallback branch. Call Path Why a Tool Is Invisible Naming and Dynamic Registration Parallelism, Timeouts, and Budgets Two Clipping Channels for Results MCP Integration Protocol and Provider Removed and Merged Limits

title: Workspaces and the Working Directory
summary: Per-user workspace isolation, the difference between the Cloud's single directory and the Desktop's multiple roots, location and rules, file operations, usage statistics, and the local boundary.
text: Workspaces and the Working Directory Per-user workspace isolation, the difference between the Cloud's single directory and the Desktop's multiple roots, location and rules, file operations, usage statistics, and the local boundary. In a Server deployment every user has exactly one cloud workspace, and the agent's file tools are rooted at it. The Desktop and Android can register several workspaces (local directories, the cloud workspace, and remote device workspaces reached through device interlink) and resolve each root by workspaceid. Tool execution is always bounded by the path fence. Isolation Policy Isolation has exactly one layer: per user. Files of different users are fully isolated; neither side can see the other. Server: a user has exactly one cloud workspace; there is no second "personal files / agent files" layer, and user, agent instance, and cloud workspace map one to one. Desktop / Android: the same user may own several workspace roots, but each root is still bounded by that user and never shared across users. Location | Form | Location | How to access | | --- | --- | --- | | Desktop (default) | A persistent directory on your machine; several local / cloud / interlink remote workspaces can be registered at once | Browse with your system file manager; the agent reads and writes directly | | Server | A single per-user directory under the server data root | Upload, download, and edit through the "Working directory" area in the Desktop's left sidebar | Three firm rules: | Rule | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Unique in the Cloud | In a Server deployment each user has exactly one cloud workspace at a time; no second directory is opened for another agent | | Multiple roots on the Desktop | The Desktop / Android can add and switch several workspace roots; one tool call only acts on the current workspace | | Fixed | In a Server deployment the cloud directory is fixed once assigned; a user cannot add, delete, or replace it | | Relative paths | Paths shown in the interface and exchanged through APIs are always workspace-relative; absolute paths are never exposed | What It Carries Data isolation: a user can only access their own workspace; path checks use the user root as the boundary, and out-of-bounds reads and writes are rejected; in a Server deployment the agent's file tools are rooted at that user's cloud directory and no second root is derived. File persistence: the workspace is not cleaned automatically, so the files put in and the files the agent generates are kept long term. Long-lived files go in the workspace and transient transfers in the temporary directory. Root of configuration: the workspace is also the root of "what the agent can see" — the skills directory, knowledge files, and global settings, which the agent reads at startup to initialize. The agent's model, prompts, tools, and approval mode are bound through admin-side presets and managed on the settings page, not by hand-writing files in the workspace. File Operations Access: in the Desktop, use the file manager directly, or the "Working directory" area in the app's left sidebar with its file tree and toolbar. In the Desktop's left sidebar, below the workspace, there is a "Working directory" area with a file tree and an upload / create / refresh / multi-select toolbar. In conversation: hand files to the agent, or have it read and write files in the workspace directly. Reference into chat: pick "Reference into chat" from a file row's menu to bring the file into the input area. Download (Desktop): select files in the tree to download; multi-select bundles them into an archive. File organization: create subdirectories by project or topic, one directory per project, and split source material from output inside it; put files the agent should analyze into the workspace first, then mention the path or filename in the message; the reports and scripts the agent generates land in the same tree. Delete files no longer needed and give files meaningful names. Usage Statistics The bottom of the file area shows used capacity, file count, and directory count. Statistics use bounded traversal and are marked as a lower bound for very large directories. On a Server deployment with a quota configured, uploads are rejected with a prompt to clean up once the limit is hit; without a quota, only used capacity is shown, with no quota denominator. The Desktop's Local Boundary The Desktop runs locally, and its working directory is a persistent directory on your machine rather than a temporary sandbox: Contents persist and are not periodically cleaned. Whether the agent can access local paths depends on local security settings. It is flexible, but the directory boundaries need checking first. Limits In a Server deployment the cloud workspace cannot be moved to another directory, nor can a second one be added; the Desktop / Android can register several workspace roots. The agent instance and the cloud workspace are still one-to-one: each user has one agent instance; the Server has one cloud workspace, while the Desktop can have multiple roots. Files no longer split into a "personal container" and an "agent container"; that layering is gone, and the user and the agent share the same workspace. The API exchanges paths relative to the workspace root, and absolute paths are not exposed. Isolation Policy Location What It Carries File Operations Usage Statistics The Desktop's Local Boundary Limits

title: Sessions and Rounds
summary: The four-layer numbering of threads, user rounds, model rounds, and entries, plus counting conventions, idempotency and queueing, timeline entries, and interface reading.
text: Sessions and Rounds The four-layer numbering of threads, user rounds, model rounds, and entries, plus counting conventions, idempotency and queueing, timeline entries, and interface reading. The numbering keeps "how many times the user asked" separate from "how many steps the agent took". Statistics, replay, queueing, and token accounting all run on this coordinate system. Structure | Concept | What it is | Decided by | | --- | --- | --- | | Thread / session | The main body of a continuous stretch of execution and dialogue; one session id runs through scheduling, locking, and state | Starting a thread starts a session; a subagent is an independent session traced back by its parent session id | | User round | One accepted human input | Incremented in the session on acceptance; a uniqueness constraint guarantees "one root per round" | | Model round | One model call of the engine's main loop, which may include a batch of tool calls | Incremented once per sample of the main loop | | Entry | The smallest renderable record on the timeline | Upserted by a stable entry id when it is written | The coordinates of the four layers: | Coordinate | Meaning | | --- | --- | | User round | Which user round it belongs to | | Model round | Which model call within that round (empty before sampling begins) | | Round id | The persistent id of that user round, used as the prefix of the entry identifier | | Target round | This round was started by the target driver rather than by a person, so a goal action that needs human authority is not started twice | Counting Conventions One model round = one model call, not "one action". Tool calls belong to a batch within the same model round and are not counted as separate model rounds. One model round produces exactly one visible output item: refreshing several times within the same model round only updates that item and never appends duplicate bubbles. A tool-batch entry on the timeline is not an independent model round. Each tool call is its own entry (merging "in progress → done / failed" by call id), so the number of steps is usually larger than the number of model rounds. A continuation round does not consume a user round: a continuation that carries a root-round reference (for example, the target driver taking over) reuses the same user round and only adds model rounds within it. A user round publishes a change only when it is genuinely newly created; a replayed acceptance is an idempotent no-op that produces no new round and notifies no subscribers. Idempotency and Queueing | Mechanism | Convention | | --- | --- | | Submit idempotency | The same client message id reuses the existing round, so a network retry does not create an extra round | | Serialization within a session | The session lock is isolated per session, with a 120-second timeout and a 5-second heartbeat; an abnormal exit releases it on timeout | | Queueing | Since Desktop v1.0.0 the frontend local waiting queue (waitingturns) holds messages sent while running above the input box and sends them when the current turn settles; switching away hands them to the engine queue. The Cloud build still uses the engine session queue (on by default, in-order execution) | | Turning queueing off | In the Cloud build, a message sent while running is judged "user busy" and not queued (the Server warns at startup); the Desktop build is unaffected | | Background delivery | Scheduled messages take the forced-enqueue path so they are not lost while competing for the lock with human messages | Timeline Entries A session records only events with timeline value: | Entry type | State flow | | --- | --- | | Tool call | In progress → done / failed (merged by the same call id) | | Model call | Numbered by model round | | Visible reply | The output item of that model round | | Approval | Waiting → decided | | Subagent message | Uses the producer-supplied message id as a persistent identity, so a replay never becomes a new entry | | Queue ledger | Engine side: pending → running (upserted on the same entry); the interface skips it. Desktop local waiting turns do not enter the timeline until sent | Not recorded: transport deltas, heartbeats, progress, context occupancy, workspace updates, model usage, and streaming retries, together with lifecycle receipts (ended, status, model response, and so on — failure details are carried by the round's terminal state). These are visible in the stream but do not become empty timeline entries. Interface Reading The chat page shows one user round per row (12 per page by default, up to 20), folding everything between the final reply into a "working process". The most recent round's working process is expanded by default (opening a thread shows what just happened); earlier rounds stay collapsed. Expansion fetches that user round's persistent entries on demand rather than pulling the entire history into the frontend. The entry-by-entry panorama lives in the "thread trace" view (80 per page by default, up to 100), with long bodies fetched in 8 KB chunks. The directory list reads the tail of each round (highest user round, that round's state, a recent-activity summary, and the backfill cursor), querying a page of sessions in one batch. Starting and Reusing Sessions When to start a new session: changing topic; needing to apply new agent settings, a prompt template, or long-term memory (an existing session's prompt is already frozen); or when the context has grown long and is starting to lose early detail. When to keep the current one: the same task is still unfinished, or you need to reference earlier output. Continuing does not recompute the base; it only adds rounds. How to point at "a certain step": give the coordinates "user round + model round", or the entry id directly; for tool batches give the entry sequence number only and do not call it "round N". Common Misreadings "One round = one question and answer" — one user round can contain many model rounds, and each model round can carry a batch of tool calls. "Step count = round count" — they are not equal; steps (entries) are usually more. "A session and a thread are two things" — in this system they are the same: the session is the carrier of the conversation and its records, and the thread is its executing body. "Submitting again charges an extra round" — a retry with the same client message id is idempotent. "A subagent's input shows up in the parent session" — a sub-session's opening user message is hidden by default and skips automatic memory extraction, so it does not pollute your memory. "Token statistics = the provider's bill" — a session records context occupancy (trusting only the value the model reports), not a billing figure. Structure Counting Conventions Idempotency and Queueing Timeline Entries Interface Reading Starting and Reusing Sessions Common Misreadings

title: Runtime and Online Status
summary: The six runtime states of a session, interface badges and indicators, how to judge a stuck session, and the sequence for handling inconsistent state.
text: Runtime and Online Status The six runtime states of a session, interface badges and indicators, how to judge a stuck session, and the sequence for handling inconsistent state. Alongside its history, a session maintains a set of runtime states — running, waiting for approval, waiting for your input, interrupting, idle, and not loaded — from which the interface derives a summary snapshot. Session States The first layer is what the session is doing at this moment. | State | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Running | Actively working | | Waiting for approval | Paused on an action that needs your go-ahead | | Waiting for your input | The agent is waiting for you to add information | | Interrupting | Being interrupted | | Idle | Nothing to do, waiting for your next message | | Not loaded | Not yet loaded into memory | The second layer is a summary snapshot the interface reads directly: whether output is still streaming, whether the session is waiting, whether it is loaded, whether it is active, and whether it has already reached a terminal state. Interface Presentation Session list: the status badges come straight from runtime state — a green dot means an active session, a spinning icon means running, and a waiting icon means waiting for approval or input. Session detail: the status indicator tells you which stage you are at, whether you can send a new message, and whether any approval is pending. Diagnosing a Stuck Session Runtime state is the starting point for troubleshooting. | You want to know | Look at | | --- | --- | | Whether it is still running | Whether output is still streaming | | Whether it is waiting | Whether it is in a waiting state | | Whether it has finished | Whether it has reached a terminal state | | Whether it can still be observed | Whether it is loaded and active | A single coarse running / not-running flag cannot tell "still streaming" apart from "waiting for approval", and it says nothing about whether the session is loaded or has reached a terminal state. Read the full set of snapshot fields. Handling Inconsistent State If the interface and the actual state do not match: 1. Wait a few seconds to see whether it recovers on its own. 2. Refresh the page or restart the app. 3. Call POST /wunder/auth/me/resetworkstate (no UI entry since v1.0.0). Limits Waiting for approval is a pause, not an ending — it is still within the session lifecycle. State belongs on the list and event pages too, not only the detail page. The event stream carries the timeline while the runtime snapshot carries the present moment; they are not the same layer. Session States Interface Presentation Diagnosing a Stuck Session Handling Inconsistent State Limits

title: Prompts and Skills
summary: Composition and freezing of the system prompt, the three layers of skills, switching template packs and where changes apply, and the division of responsibility.
text: Prompts and Skills Composition and freezing of the system prompt, the three layers of skills, switching template packs and where changes apply, and the division of responsibility. An agent's behavior is decided by two things: its system prompt (who it is, how it thinks, what principles it holds) and its skills (the concrete method it follows for a class of task). System Prompt The system prompt is the agent's working manual. It sets out the role it plays, the engineering principles it follows, how it uses tools, how it calls on skills, and what memory context it remembers. The system prompt is fixed when the session is created and stays frozen afterward. This keeps the agent's behavior consistent within the same session. Skills A skill is an operating manual for the agent. It bundles a full method, execution scripts, examples and resources, and the constraints and boundaries that apply. When it needs to, the agent reads the complete skill document. A skill packages a method for a class of task, so similar tasks follow the same method. Skills come in three layers. | Layer | Description | Editable | | --- | --- | --- | | Built-in | Shipped with the system | Read-only | | Custom | Created by a user or administrator | Editable | | External | Imported from outside | Depends on the source | Prompt Template Packs wunder supports several prompt template packs: a Chinese pack (Chinese style by default), an English pack (English style by default), and custom packs tailored as needed. To switch, open the agent settings, find "Prompt template", pick one, and save. When it takes effect: a new conversation uses the new template while existing conversations are unchanged. Changing a template and seeing no change in the current conversation is expected; starting a new conversation picks it up. To build a custom template, copy a built-in one, edit the sections (role, principles, additional notes, and so on), and save it to use. Placeholder Resource Paths Resource paths inside a skill document are written as placeholders rather than hard-coded paths. A skill lives in a different actual location in each runtime form, so the system substitutes the correct path when the skill is used. Division of Responsibility | | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | Prompt | Defines the long-lived, stable boundary of behavior | | Skill | Defines the additional execution protocol for a class of task | | Memory | Defines the long-term facts injected when a session initializes | The three work together, and their responsibilities are not mixed. Template and Skill Management A template has a clear role, concise principles (keep the important constraints rather than piling them on), no internal contradictions, and is tuned against real results. Skills are managed on the "Tools" page: see installed skills, enable or disable them, create a skill for a particular working scenario, and share one with the team. Combining prompt templates, skills, and models produces agents of different styles: a coding assistant, a copywriter, a data analyst, a translation expert. Limits Changing a template does not affect the current conversation right away; it only affects new conversations. A skill is not just a documentation file; it is a runtime resource the agent can actively read. Memory does not rewrite the prompt every round; it is injected once at initialization. System Prompt Skills Prompt Template Packs Placeholder Resource Paths Division of Responsibility Template and Skill Management Limits

title: Long-term Memory
summary: Injection and freezing rules for structured memory fragments, what memory can hold, initialization injection versus runtime recall, and how it differs from the knowledge base.
headings: Memory and the Knowledge Base Are Not the Same
text: Long-term Memory Injection and freezing rules for structured memory fragments, what memory can hold, initialization injection versus runtime recall, and how it differs from the knowledge base. Memory follows stability over flexibility: it is injected once when the session is created, frozen while running, and supplemented by recall when material is needed. Core Rules 1. Injected once when the session is created: long-term memory is written into the system prompt once, when the conversation starts. 2. Frozen while running: later turns do not change the system prompt. 3. Supplemented by recall when needed: while running, recall adds material, but it does not rewrite the foundation. The reason it is not updated every round: rewriting the system prompt each round would make the agent's behavior unstable (drifting as the conversation goes on), lower the cache hit rate (making it slower), and make problems hard to trace (you could not say what background it was working from at the time). Structure Memory is made of structured fragments, not one long free-form passage. A fragment is found by lookup, replaced without affecting the rest, marked invalid when outdated, and carries traceable version relationships. What Memory Can Hold Who you are: preferences and habits, work background, past decisions. Organizational knowledge: team rules and standards, project background, domain expertise. Personalization: adjusting the answer style to your preferences, referring to your past context, and giving targeted suggestions. Initialization Injection vs Runtime Recall | | Initialization injection | Runtime recall | | --- | --- | --- | | Timing | When the session is created | During the conversation | | How | Written into the system prompt | Added as a tool result | | Effect | Becomes the session's cognitive foundation | Does not rewrite the foundation | | Scope | The life of the whole session | The current round | Managing Memory View: see the current memory in the agent settings. Add: tell the agent "remember this preference," or add it by hand in settings. Delete: remove fragments that are outdated or unneeded. Update: add a new fragment to replace an old one. When it takes effect: a new conversation uses the latest memory at once; an existing conversation is unaffected and keeps using the memory from when it was created. So after updating memory, you need to start a new conversation for it to apply. Memory and the Knowledge Base Are Not the Same | | Memory | Knowledge base | | --- | --- | --- | | Content | Structured personal / organizational facts | Documents, material, and standards | | When used | Injected at initialization | Retrieved while running | | Update frequency | Relatively stable | Can be updated often | | Good for | Preferences, background, decision records | Reference material, technical documents | Limits Memory is not updated every round; it is injected once at initialization. The results of recall are not written back into the system prompt; they are only a temporary supplement. More memory is not better: too much crowds the context and can interfere with judgment. Core Rules Structure What Memory Can Hold Initialization Injection vs Runtime Recall Managing Memory Memory and the Knowledge Base Are Not the Same Limits

title: Quota and Token Usage
summary: How the 1-credit-per-model-request and 1000-per-day grant are issued and deducted, and what the token metrics observe.
text: Quota and Token Usage How the 1-credit-per-model-request and 1000-per-day grant are issued and deducted, and what the token metrics observe. Quota limits how many model requests you can make. Regular users receive 1000 credits per day, the same regardless of organization or level. Unused credits accumulate. The grant is applied once on the day's first use or account adjustment; days when nothing was used are not backfilled. Each real model request costs 1 credit, including the next model call inside a tool loop, compaction summaries, and failed retries. Streaming chunks, standalone tool execution, and history replay cost no credits. A request consumes a credit even if it fails; when the balance is insufficient, no new model request is dispatched. Administrators and unregistered virtual users are not limited by quota. Viewing and Adjusting On the user side, "My Profile" shows the current balance and the daily grant. Administrators can set the balance directly in "User management → Settings", or grant and deduct credits: A value set directly is the final balance after the day's grant is carried over. A grant increases "cumulative granted", while a deduction counts toward "cumulative used"; an operation is rejected when the balance is insufficient. The account shows several numbers: available credits, cumulative granted, cumulative used and administrative deductions, the daily grant, and the most recent grant date. Multiple sessions share one user credit account, and concurrent requests cannot overdraw it. User levels still accumulate experience but no longer award credits. On the first upgrade, an old token-balance account is initialized to 1000 credits and is not converted from its historical token count; a restart afterward does not reset the balance either. Token Observation Token usage describes a model's input, output, reasoning, and context size, and it never affects the credit deduction. A short request and a long request both cost 1 credit. The token metrics you can see include: Context occupancy: the context size most recently observed. The cumulative model tokens consumed within one user request. Model usage events, plus the request count, whether it was charged, the credit consumed in that turn, and the account snapshot for each real model request. In a session, "model request count" and "credit consumption" are two different metrics: for a regular user, one billable model request normally increases each by one; in an exempt case such as an administrator, the request count still increases but credit consumption stays at zero. The account snapshot only shows the balance at that moment and does not represent how much this request deducted. Old credit records are kept only for reading history. Viewing and Adjusting Token Observation

title: Goal Mode
summary: Fields of a session-level persistent goal, the four phases and the continuation gate, the in-process arming flag, model-side operations, and the available entry points.
text: Goal Mode Fields of a session-level persistent goal, the four phases and the continuation gate, the in-process arming flag, model-side operations, and the available entry points. Goal mode hangs a goal on a session and pairs it with a driver that lives only in the current process. Whenever the session goes idle, the driver submits the next continuation (a goal round), and each round spends one unit of the model-round budget; whether it keeps going or stops is decided by the budget, the phase, and whether the goal is blocked. Goal Fields | Field | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Objective | What to do, up to 4,000 characters | | Phase | One of active, paused, blocked, complete — these four and nothing else | | Continuation-round budget (maxgoalrounds) | The most automatic continuations that may run; defaults to 256 when the goal is created | | Started rounds (roundsstarted) | Only ever increases; it is never reset backwards | | Revision | Increments on every change; an update must carry the goal id and its exact current revision, and a mismatch is rejected (compare-and-set on revision) | | Blocked reason | When blocked, a machine code (blockedcode) plus a plain-language explanation (blockedmessage) | When It Applies | Situation | What to do | | --- | --- | | Long tasks with a clear completion condition that the model should push forward over several rounds | Use goal mode | | Something a single round of Q&A can resolve | Just send a message | | Work that needs you in the decision loop often | Talk directly, and add the question panel when needed | | You only want the current round to go deeper | An ordinary round is enough; a model round has no built-in one-step-one-answer limit | Phases | Phase | Meaning | How it is entered | How it is left | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | active | Able to continue | The user creates a goal, or resumes one | paused / blocked / complete | | paused | Sitting still; a person can resume at any time | A manual pause, or a continuation round that was interrupted | Resume | | blocked | Automatic continuation stops | The model self-reports the same blocking condition once at least 3 consecutive continuation rounds have run; or the driver fails to enqueue (queue-failed) | Resume (after the blocking condition is resolved) | | complete | Achieved | The model or a person marks it complete, and only when it is truly done | Reopen with a new goal | Whether the next round starts depends on a single gate: the phase is active, the goal is armed inside the process, and roundsstarted has not reached the budget — all three must hold to continue. A person's message always wins; a continuation round never competes with a person for the session. Budget Unit and Round Boundaries The budget is counted in model rounds, not tokens. The system does not track how many tokens a goal burns, there is no token budget, and there is no design in which the budget runs out and drops the goal into some restricted state. There is no cooldown between rounds. As soon as the session is idle, the driver immediately decides whether to send the next round. "Blocked" does not mean "hard": difficulty, uncertainty, and unfinished work are not reasons to report blocked. The agent must name a concrete blocking condition that persists across rounds. Arming Is Not Persisted Whether a goal is armed is an in-process flag and is not stored in the database. After a process restart, a session restore, or a fork, the driver will not pick up automatically even if the phase is still active — it has to be armed again with an explicit goal carrying action=resume. When asking why a goal stopped moving, first check whether it is still armed. Model-Side Operations Only the user can start a goal: /goal , the goal bar, or the goal API creates one; the model cannot create or replace a goal. The model side manages an existing goal through one strict-action goal tool. | Tool | Effect | | --- | --- | | goal | Uses action=get to read the current goal, including the id and revision required for later operations, and uses edit, pause, resume, complete, or blocked to update one. Updates need the goal id and current revision, and reporting blocked is rejected before the minimum round count is reached | Authority does not come from anything the model writes: human entry points stamp source = "human" onto the turn and the goal-round driver stamps goalround. Edit, pause, and resume are allowed only in a person's round; complete and report-blocked are additionally allowed in the goal's own automatic continuation rounds. The runtime rejects any model attempt to create a goal and points the user to /goal or the goal bar. The Desktop does not expose the goal tool for users to pick (it is a hidden built-in capability); the runtime injects it per session, and the Cloud (web) and the CLI reuse the same injection. Entry Points | Entry | Location | | --- | --- | | API | GET/PUT/DELETE /wunder/chat/sessions/{id}/goal (user side; requires an ownership check) | | Slash command | /goal [ \|clear\|edit \|pause\|resume] | | Cloud | A goal bar in the message area | | Desktop | A goal banner above the input box, with inline editing | | CLI | The /goal command | | Admin | No goal UI (the governance surface offers no goal operations) | Points Often Misread A goal does not stop on a token limit; it looks only at the round budget, the phase, and arming. After a service restart an active goal does not resume on its own; a resume action is needed to arm it again. The model cannot mark a goal blocked at will: the same blocking condition must persist across at least 3 continuation rounds. Only the user can start a goal. The model-side goal tool's actions are strictly get, edit, pause, resume, complete, and blocked; it has no create action. The Admin has no goal panel; use the Cloud, the Desktop, or the CLI. Clearing a goal does not undo work already done: messages, tool results, and file changes already stored are kept. Goal Fields When It Applies Phases Budget Unit and Round Boundaries Arming Is Not Persisted Model-Side Operations Entry Points Points Often Misread

title: Companion System
summary: ZIP package and sprite-sheet specification, per-form presentation, scale and position ranges, and user versus administrator permissions.
text: Companion System ZIP package and sprite-sheet specification, per-form presentation, scale and position ranges, and user versus administrator permissions. A companion package is a ZIP holding a manifest and a sprite sheet; at runtime the row played depends on the session state. Companions take no part in execution and do not affect scheduling, so deleting one changes no functionality. Package Structure A companion package is a ZIP that holds exactly two things: a manifest and a sprite-sheet image. The manifest (pet.json) is JSON and states the companion's id, display name, and description, along with where the sprite-sheet file lives. The sprite sheet is a single image whose path the manifest gives. Size limits: the whole ZIP is at most 24 MB, and the single sprite-sheet file is at most 18 MB. Import guards against path traversal inside the archive. Companion files live in one fixed companion directory (config/data/companions/global, overridable through WUNDERCOMPANIONSROOT); embedded forms such as the Desktop and the CLI pin this directory to their own data directory. The Desktop bundles two sample companion packages and releases them into its local library on first launch; the Cloud and the Admin ship none, so an empty list there is normal. Sprite-Sheet Specification Every frame is a fixed 192 × 208 pixels, and frames of the same state line up horizontally in the same row; one state occupies one row. The row number is the state (rows 0–8): | Row | State | Row | State | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0 | idle | 5 | failed | | 1 | running-right | 6 | waiting | | 2 | running-left | 7 | running | | 3 | waving | 8 | review | | 4 | jumping | | | The session's runtime state maps to an animation row: running → running (row 7), completed → jumping (row 4), waiting → waiting (row 6), error → failed (row 5), and everything else falls back to idle (row 0). Clicking the companion plays the waving animation once. A companion package may declare fewer rows or frames: out-of-range rows or frames are degraded by a bounds check and never crash. Presentation per Form | Form | Presentation | | --- | --- | | Desktop (Windows) | Native floating window: a Win32 layered window for the selected companion, with dragging and the frame clock on a separate message thread that does not occupy the UI thread | | Desktop (Linux) | No equivalent floating window; the desktop pet exists only on Windows | | Cloud | An in-page overlay that follows the chat state | | Admin | A companion management panel: upload, edit, delete, and export global companions | | CLI | No companion UI; it only points the companion directory at the local data directory | Scale and Position | Item | Range | | --- | --- | | Stored / settings-slider scale | 0.1–1.6 (step 0.1, default 0.5) | | Render scale | 0.1–1.8 | | Position | Clamped to the screen work area with margins kept; drag results are saved | The Desktop stores the globally selected companion, the show switch, the scale, the message-hint switch and the position in a local file; the Cloud stores them in the browser, so clearing browser data resets position and preferences. Permissions The user side is read-only: four GET endpoints only — the global list, one companion's detail, its sprite sheet, and its exported package (/wunder/companions/global). Adding, changing, and deleting sit on the administrator side (/wunder/admin/companions): list, import, edit and delete, sprite sheet, export package. The import request-body limit matches the ZIP limit, both 24 MB. A "private companion" in the Cloud takes effect only in the current browser and is not uploaded to the server; a global companion is uploaded by an administrator through the Admin and is then visible to all users. The Admin is the only upload path. Limits A companion is not another kind of agent; it is only the visual shell of an agent, and one agent binds one companion. Users cannot upload a companion to the server from the Cloud; server-side companions are managed by administrators through the Admin, and private imports stay in the local browser. The Desktop on Linux has no desktop floating window — the overlay is a Win32 implementation with no Linux equivalent. Companion animation does not affect task execution: the runtime state drives the animation, not the other way around. The Desktop ships sample companion packages; the Cloud and the Admin's global library ship none, so an administrator uploads them. Package Structure Sprite-Sheet Specification Presentation per Form Scale and Position Permissions Limits

title: Boundary Handling
summary: Graduated compression on context overflow, reconnect and event replay after a disconnect, tool failure handling by type, and queueing with priority.
text: Boundary Handling Graduated compression on context overflow, reconnect and event replay after a disconnect, tool failure handling by type, and queueing with priority. Each failure type has its own path: a failure in one link does not drag the others down, every failure keeps a recovery route, and problems of the same kind can be categorized, reproduced, and verified. Context Overflow As a conversation grows longer and tool results pile up, the total token count approaches the model's ceiling. Compression runs progressively in four levels: | Level | What it does | Loss | | --- | --- | --- | | Level 1 | Remove intermediate tool results | Very low | | Level 2 | Summarize the conversation history | Medium | | Level 3 | Remove earlier parts of the conversation | Higher | | Level 4 | Emergency degradation | Very high | The system prompt never takes part in compression and stays frozen, so compression never changes the agent's behavioral setup. On long conversations, watch context usage and compress proactively with /compact when needed; start a new session once a topic is done. Disconnect and Reconnect After a disconnect caused by network jitter, the interface shows a prompt first and then reconnects automatically with exponential backoff (1 s → 2 s → 4 s → 8 s → 16 s, up to 32 s). Events that were not pushed during the disconnect are cached and replayed once the reconnect succeeds; the interface only prompts for a manual refresh if the replay also fails. When the interface shows "connection lost", wait for the automatic reconnect instead of refreshing repeatedly. Tool Failure | Failure type | Handling | | --- | --- | | Wrong parameters | The agent corrects the parameters itself and retries | | Permission denied | Execution stops and waits for approval | | Temporary error (file locked, network jitter) | Automatic retry | | System error | Limited retry plus degradation | Read the failure notice for the cause and adjust as it suggests (for example, give the correct file path); if it keeps failing, ask an administrator to check the system logs. Oversized Tool Output Three layers of containment: | Layer | Role | | --- | --- | | Execution budget | Caps the size of a single output | | Result trimming | Keeps the head and tail when the limit is exceeded | | Pre-model check | Trims once more before the input reaches the model | A trimmed result tells the agent explicitly that it was cut, so the agent can switch strategy. Queueing and Priority When a conversation is busy, new requests are not turned away but queued and run in turn once it is free. Priority runs from high to low: administrators > high priority > normal > low priority. Limits An agent answering does not mean everything is fine; check whether it stays stable over time and whether it reports failures when they happen. Retrying applies to some error types only. Boundary cases show up often in long conversations and complex tasks. If there is no response for a long time, try cancelling or resetting first; if the state is clearly wrong, call POST /wunder/auth/me/resetworkstate (since v1.0.0 the Settings page exposes no such entry); if it keeps happening, ask an administrator to troubleshoot. Context Overflow Disconnect and Reconnect Tool Failure Oversized Tool Output Queueing and Priority Limits

title: Chat WebSocket
summary: The `/wunder/chat/ws` handshake, client message kinds, server replies, and how to reconnect.
text: Chat WebSocket The /wunder/chat/ws handshake, client message kinds, server replies, and how to reconnect. # Chat WebSocket /wunder/chat/ws is both the event stream and the control channel: starting a run, resuming after a drop, watching, cancelling and returning approvals all happen on one connection. Chat and the desktop live session share it. Handshake 1. Create a session and keep its id. 2. Open the WebSocket. 3. Send connect to shake hands. 4. Receive ready. 5. Send start to begin a run. 6. Consume event until the turn's terminal signal. Message kinds | kind | Purpose | | --- | --- | | connect | Handshake and protocol negotiation | | start | Begin one run | | resume | Replay events missed during a drop | | watch | Observe a session only | | cancel | Cancel the current run | | approval | Return an approval decision | | ping | Keepalive | The server replies with ready, event, error, pong. turnterminal is the terminal signal of a single turn and works well as the client's settling condition. Conventions start must carry the session id; the body field is content, not the HTTP endpoint's question. resume (replay) and watch (observe) are different actions; one does not replace the other. Only approvals delivered over this connection are handled on it. After a drop, reconnect to the same URL and send resume or watch. The desktop reconnects automatically. Chat WebSocket Handshake Message kinds Conventions

title: MCP Endpoint
summary: The two directions — the address and two built-in tools when exposing wunder, and the configuration order when connecting an external MCP service.
text: MCP Endpoint The two directions — the address and two built-in tools when exposing wunder, and the configuration order when connecting an external MCP service. # MCP Endpoint wunder can expose itself as an MCP service and act as an MCP client for external services. The two directions have different entry points and settings; tool-level registration, packing and routing are on MCP. Exposing wunder The outward entry is one address over Streamable HTTP. 1. An external system connects with the MCP protocol. 2. wunder negotiates the protocol version automatically, picking a range both sides support when talking to older servers. 3. The system calls a specific tool. Two tools are built in: excute (run an agent task and return the final reply — the name really is spelled this way) and doc2md (parse a document and return Markdown). While running a task the endpoint computes the tool set fresh and removes itself, so an endpoint-driven agent cannot call back into it. Connecting an external service 1. Declare the service name, address and transport (Streamable HTTP only). 2. Switch it on and confirm in the Admin that the tool list can be fetched. 3. Grant the tools to the agents that need them. External services usually carry database queries, exports, or knowledge retrieval. Tools register as server@tool, or collapse into one tool when the server is marked as packed — see MCP. Debug order If the tool list will not load, check the address and transport first, then whether the service is enabled and whether an allow-list blocks it. If the list loads but the model cannot call the tools, check ability selection and model capability filtering. MCP Endpoint Exposing wunder Connecting an external service Debug order

title: WeChat iLink Channel
summary: Choosing between `weixin` and the older WeChat channels, QR onboarding, required and optional settings, and the order to debug missing messages.
text: WeChat iLink Channel Choosing between weixin and the older WeChat channels, QR onboarding, required and optional settings, and the order to debug missing messages. # WeChat iLink Channel weixin is its own channel and its parameters are not interchangeable with the earlier two. Pick by scenario first. Choosing | Scenario | Channel | | --- | --- | | WeCom app callback | wechat | | WeChat official-account callback | wechatmp | | iLink-protocol WeChat capabilities | weixin | The differences: weixin long-polls for updates, must echo the conversation identifier on each reply, gets its bot token by QR scan, and handles media through a CDN with its own encryption; the other two use webhook callbacks and platform-native media. QR onboarding 1. Pick weixin in channel settings and generate a QR code. 2. Scan it with WeChat. 3. Wait for confirmation. 4. The bot token, bot id, user id and endpoint are filled in automatically. 5. Save the account — without saving, long polling never starts. QR codes expire; regenerate if needed. Settings Required: endpoint, bot token, bot id, plus the long-connection switch. Optional: CDN address, bot type, allowed caller scope, polling and request timeouts, backoff after repeated failures, routing tag. Debugging | Symptom | Check first | | --- | --- | | No messages arrive | Account active, long connection on, token and bot id valid, runtime session not expired | | Reply rejected for a missing conversation identifier | This reply lost the inbound message's identifier; confirm the reply goes to the same conversation and the identifier was kept | | Media missing | Media enabled, CDN reachable, decryption key correct, attachment under the size limit | | Session expiring constantly | Usually a stale login: rescan for a new token and save | Relationship to other channels Same engine, same tools and permissions; a channel is just an entry point. Bindings and logs live in Settings → Channels, and the Admin only reflects channel configuration inside preset agent templates. WeChat iLink Channel Choosing QR onboarding Settings Debugging Relationship to other channels

title: Multi-Device Interlink
summary: Device states after signing in to the Server, the workspace shadow projection, tiered approval for cross-device control, and the drop and permission boundaries.
headings: What it deliberately does not do
text: Multi-Device Interlink Device states after signing in to the Server, the workspace shadow projection, tiered approval for cross-device control, and the drop and permission boundaries. # Multi-Device Interlink Desktop and Android are first of all local workbenches that run offline. After signing in to the Server you can reach cloud agents and threads without opening a local port; once the user enables local sharing, Cloud can go through the Server relay to view and operate that device's workspaces and threads within the granted scope. The CLI exposes the same ability for hands-on and scripted use. Three states, not one | State | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Signed in | Cloud resources are reachable | | Tunnel online | Cloud can operate this local device | | This operation is authorized | The specific write or exec is allowed | The first sign-in only yields a separate device session; local files and threads are not opened automatically. The sharing level (off, summary, full) is chosen in account settings, and the Admin can tighten it further. Device states online (idle), busy (running), away (online but idle for a while), reconnecting, offline. The Server records the signed-in session, the tunnel connection and the available capabilities separately, so the three can disagree. Capabilities | Capability | What it means | | --- | --- | | Mutual workspace view | A local workspace appears in Cloud as a shadow projection of metadata (thread index, directory summary, scheduled tasks, usage); file contents are not mirrored and are pulled on demand over the tunnel | | Cloud controls local | Queries, session control, workspace writes and tool execution are opened in tiers; sensitive ones go through a local human-in-the-loop approval and are audited | | Local controls Cloud | Desktop, Android and the CLI treat Cloud as a peer node: switch device, browse Cloud threads, send messages, read the event stream | | Several devices | The device directory distinguishes desktop, phone, CLI and web; a signed-in phone appears as a phone node that Cloud can drive under capability and approval | Entry points | Form | Entry | | --- | --- | | Desktop | Account settings (sign-in and sharing level), cloud agents and threads, local approval dialog | | Cloud | Sidebar lists local and cloud workspaces together: the default directory as "device name - local workspace", named ones as "device name - workspace name" | | CLI | cloud subcommands: devices, ws, threads, thread, send, watch, audit, approve; cloud status summarises tunnel, pending approvals, other devices and usage | Tiers and approval | Tier | Operations | Approval | | --- | --- | --- | | Read-only | device summary, shadow refresh, workspace list / search / read, thread list and detail | none | | Read-only (binary) | reading binary files | none, audited | | Session | create thread, send message, cancel, answer | local approval when acting on a local device; account auth when acting on your own cloud thread | | Workspace write | write, mkdir, move, copy, delete | forced, cannot be lowered | | Execution | allow-listed command exec, spawning subagents | forced, disabled by default in the device capability set, can be enabled | Workspace writes back up first to workspace/.interlinkbackup/ / (last 50 generations) and report checksums before and after. Execution is off by default and approvals are never remembered. Boundaries No public entry: a reverse tunnel; the local side only makes an outbound connection and never listens. Least capability: each remote operation must be declared, read-only by default. One switch: the user holds the kill switch; the Admin can narrow it further. Drops and recovery Desktop reconnects with backoff. While the Server stays up, an unsent bounded queue is delivered after reconnect; commands already sent, running or awaiting approval fail explicitly when the old connection ends, so nothing runs twice. After a Server restart, leftover commands settle as "server restarted" instead of waiting forever; command bodies are not persisted, so parameters are never rebuilt from a summary and writes are never redone automatically. Queries can be reissued; verify the actual result before reissuing a write. What it deliberately does not do Local and cloud threads are not merged: this is remote operation, not sync. No full workspace mirroring or two-way sync, only metadata projection plus on-demand pulls. No graphical remote control; the granularity stops at the engine and file APIs. No NAT traversal; all traffic is relayed by the Server, and Desktop and the CLI never talk to each other directly. Remote reads return up to 256 KiB inline, with bounded chunking beyond that; direct Cloud execution has no device data channel, so larger reads and writes must be split. Cloud offers no binary upload, archive or batch file operations. Multi-Device Interlink Three states, not one Device states Capabilities Entry points Tiers and approval Boundaries Drops and recovery What it deliberately does not do
